section: Caching Tiers: Keeping Hot Data in Memory
hook: One home-screen load reads a profile, 50 friend names and 20 counters. Now multiply by hundreds of millions.
title: One home screen, dozens of reads: why every giant caches
body: Take a global app with 1 billion users. One home-screen load reads a profile, 50 friend names, 20 post counters and some settings. Multiply by hundreds of millions of daily users and the database faces an enormous read rate. Durable stores are slow and expensive per read compared to memory. So almost every large company lands on the same answer: put **caches** in front of storage, and let most reads never reach the database.
takeaway: Durable storage is for keeping data. Memory is for serving it.
deeper:
**Three payoffs:** Memory on a nearby server answers in well under a millisecond, while a database read touching disk and replicas takes several milliseconds, and far more at the tail. Every hit is a query the database never serves. And a memory read burns far less CPU than parsing SQL, taking locks and walking B-tree pages.

**The bill:** A cache is another system to run and more memory to buy. Worse, it can disagree with the source of truth. Most caching bugs live in that gap between the copy and the original.

**The scale traps:** Once caches carry real load, three new problems appear. A popular key expires and thousands of requests stampede the database at once. One celebrity key overwhelms the single server that owns it. An empty cache after a restart or failover suddenly faces full traffic.

**The catch:** The cache that saves your database can become the thing your database cannot live without.

quiz.q: Your app's home screen reads about 70 keys per load for hundreds of millions of daily users. The database team wants to keep adding replicas. What is the cheaper lever, and what new risk does it bring?
quiz.a: Cache the hot reads in memory: far less CPU and latency per read than the database. The new risk is staleness, the cache disagreeing with the source of truth.

mcq.q: Why do large companies put caches in front of durable storage?
options: Memory serves repeated reads far faster and cheaper than the database
Caches make stored data more durable than the database
Caches remove the need to replicate the database
Memory is cheaper per gigabyte than disk
mcq.why: A durable store is slow and expensive per read; memory answers repeated reads in well under a millisecond with far less CPU.

hook: You can throw away any cache entry at any moment and nothing breaks. So why do most caching bugs still happen?
title: A cache is a copy you're allowed to lose
body:
Delete any entry from a cache and the system still returns correct answers. A **cache** is a fast, smaller copy of data whose real home, the **source of truth**, lives somewhere slower. Anything missing is simply read again from the source. That one property shapes every caching design.

The danger runs the other way. The copy can disagree with the source, and that gap, **stale data**, is where most caching bugs live.
takeaway: Losing a cache entry costs speed. Keeping a wrong one costs correctness.
deeper:
**What disposability buys:** Because the copy is expendable, you can make choices no database could. Meta sends memcache reads over UDP and treats dropped packets as misses. Nodes restart freely, and memory pressure just evicts entries. None of that would be acceptable for data of record.

**What it does not buy:** Disposable covers correctness, not capacity. An empty cache still gives right answers, but the database may not survive serving all of them. Big caches quietly become load-bearing.

**Where bugs come from:** Every write to the source opens a window in which the cache may hold the old value. Three races widen it: a slow reader filling an old value after a delete, a refill from a lagging replica, and a delete that never arrives.

**The review question:** Ask two separate things of any design. If the cache is lost, is the answer still correct? And does the database survive the load?

quiz.q: An engineer argues the cache needs no monitoring because 'losing it can't cause wrong answers.' Which half is right, and what did they miss?
quiz.a: Losing entries never causes wrong answers, since the source has the data. They missed staleness (entries that are wrong, not missing) and the load spike on the database when the cache empties.

mcq.q: Why can a cache drop any entry without making the system incorrect?
options: The source of truth still holds the data and can refill it
Caches replicate every entry to at least three servers
Clients keep their own copy of every value they read
The cache writes every entry to disk before serving it
mcq.why: The cache is only a copy. A missing entry becomes a miss, and the reader fetches the real value from the source of truth.

hook: At Meta, one caching server can stand in for tens of database servers. Where does that leverage come from?
title: One cache server can replace tens of database servers
body:
Database reads that touch disk and replicas take several milliseconds, much more at the tail. Memory on a nearby server answers in well under a millisecond. That is **latency**.

Then there is **offload**: every hit is a query the database never serves. Meta's CacheLib paper (2020) reports that one caching server can replace tens of backend database servers. Two numbers multiply: about 20× higher throughput per server, and hit ratios above 80 percent.
takeaway: A cache wins twice: it answers faster, and it answers instead.
deeper:
**Why it multiplies:** Throughput and hit ratio compound. A cache box handles about 20 times the requests a database box does, and with hit ratios above 80 percent only a small fraction of reads ever falls through to the database fleet.

**The tail matters most:** A Meta page load can fetch hundreds of keys, so the page waits for the slowest read. A database read that is usually a few milliseconds but sometimes much slower will land in some page's critical path constantly. Serving most reads from memory compresses the tail, not just the median. Uber's CacheFront reported p75 latency down 75 percent and p99.9 down more than 67 percent (2024).

**The catch:** Offload turns into dependency. Once the database fleet is sized for only the miss traffic, losing the cache means losing the service.

quiz.q: A page fetches 300 keys. Database reads are usually fast but occasionally very slow. Why does caching improve this page far more than average read latency suggests?
quiz.a: The page waits for its slowest read. With hundreds of reads, a slow database read almost always appears. Consistently sub-millisecond memory reads remove most slow reads from the critical path.

mcq.q: According to Meta's CacheLib paper, why can one caching server replace tens of database servers?
options: About 20× higher throughput plus hit ratios above 80 percent
About 2× higher throughput plus hit ratios above 99 percent
It stores rows compressed, so it holds 20× more data
It batches writes so the database handles fewer updates
mcq.why: Each cache server handles about 20 times the throughput, and above 80 percent of reads hit, so few requests reach the database.

predict.q: Meta's CacheLib paper compared one caching server with backend database servers. How many database servers can it replace?
options: Tens
About two
Thousands

hook: Uber serves one workload at 6 million reads/sec. How many database cores would that take without a cache?
title: Uber: 3,000 Redis cores instead of 60,000 database cores
body:
Serving a read from a database is expensive work: parse the SQL, take locks, walk B-tree pages. Serving it from memory is a key lookup and a copy.

At scale that gap becomes a budget line. Uber reported one use case at 6 million reads per second served by about 3,000 **Redis** cores, instead of an estimated 60,000 database cores (2024). Same traffic, roughly a twentieth of the compute. Caching is often a cost decision, not only a latency one.
takeaway: At millions of reads per second, the cores you avoid buying pay for the cache.
deeper:
**Where the CPU goes:** A database read runs through query parsing and planning, concurrency control, and page-oriented structures like B-trees, possibly with disk I/O. Even when the row sits in the database's own memory, it still pays the parsing and locking on every request. A cache read is a hash lookup and a memory copy.

**The source:** The number comes from CacheFront, the cache Uber built into its Docstore query engine, which serves over 40 million reads per second overall. The 60,000-core figure is an estimate for one use case, not a measured fleet.

**The other side of the ledger:** The saving is real, but so are the costs: another system to operate, extra memory, and the risk of stale data. Those costs are why invalidation and failure handling take most of the engineering effort in any serious cache.

quiz.q: The database already keeps the hot rows in its buffer pool, so a colleague says a cache adds nothing. Why can a cache still cut CPU sharply?
quiz.a: The database still parses SQL, takes locks and walks B-tree pages on every request, even for in-memory rows. A cache does a key lookup and returns bytes.

mcq.q: Uber reported about 3,000 Redis cores serving 6 million reads/sec for one use case. What was the estimated database-only alternative?
options: About 60,000 database cores
About 6,000 database cores
About 30,000 database cores
About 600,000 database cores
mcq.why: Uber estimated 60,000 database cores, roughly 20 times the Redis cores, because each database read costs far more CPU.

hook: Your hit ratio is 99 percent and the database looks bored. Someone wants to shrink it. What could go wrong?
title: A cache the database can't live without is load-bearing
body:
A cache starts as a performance tool and quietly becomes a capacity dependency. The hit ratio climbs, the database looks underused, and someone right-sizes the fleet. Now it can only handle miss traffic.

Ask in every review: if this cache were empty right now, could the database survive the load? If not, the cache is **load-bearing**. Its failure and warmup paths deserve the same care as the database itself.
takeaway: A cache the database can't survive losing is part of the database.
deeper:
**How the drift happens:** Nobody decides to make a cache load-bearing. A team adds it for latency, hit ratio rises, and a cost review trims the database. In an illustrative sizing, with 2 million reads per second and a database safe at 100,000, a 95 percent hit ratio already puts the database at its limit. Anything lower is an outage.

**Designing the failure path:** Plan for mass restarts, deploys, node failures and regional failover. Meta's Gutter pool absorbs a dead server's traffic, and Cold Cluster Warmup fills new clusters from warm peers. CacheLib restarts warm. Netflix EVCache and Uber CacheFront keep failover regions warm.

**The other answer:** DynamoDB sends constant refresh traffic to its metadata fleet even on cache hits, so that fleet never depends on a hit ratio. Or put admission control and load shedding in front of the database.

quiz.q: A cost review shows your database mostly idle behind a 99 percent hit-ratio cache and proposes cutting the fleet in half. What question should you ask first, and why?
quiz.a: Could the database survive if the cache were empty or degraded? At 99 percent it only sees misses; a partial cache failure multiplies its load, and a halved fleet would fall over.

mcq.q: What makes a cache 'load-bearing'?
options: The database cannot survive the full read load if the cache is empty
The cache holds data that exists nowhere else
The cache serves more than half of all writes
The cache runs on the same servers as the database
mcq.why: Load-bearing means capacity depends on it: without the cache, the miss traffic would exceed what the database can serve.

hook: In the most common cache pattern at big-tech scale, the cache never talks to the database. So who does?
title: Look-aside: the app checks, fills, and deletes
body: In **look-aside** (cache-aside) caching, the application owns every step. On a read it checks the cache. On a miss it reads the database and puts the value into the cache. On a write it updates the database, then deletes the cache entry rather than updating it, and the next reader refills it. Meta calls its memcache usage a demand-filled look-aside cache. It is the dominant pattern at scale.
takeaway: The database stays the truth; the cache only ever holds what someone read.
deeper:
**One key, end to end:**
1. The app calls `get(user:42)` and misses.
2. It runs SELECT for profile 42 and receives the row.
3. It calls `set(user:42, row)`.
4. Later a write runs UPDATE profile 42, gets ok, and calls `delete(user:42)`.

**Why it wins:** The database remains the source of truth, so a dead cache loses nothing. And the cache holds only data somebody actually asked for.

**The catch:** Every service must implement the logic correctly, and the gap between reading the database and filling the cache opens races. A slow reader can fill an old value after a writer's delete, or fill from a lagging replica. Look-aside with delete-on-write is only eventually consistent. Leases, versioned values, commit-log invalidation and TTLs all exist to patch those gaps. Uber's CacheFront moves the same logic into the query engine so no team can forget the delete.

quiz.q: Your look-aside cache cluster dies completely. What happens to correctness, and what happens to the database?
quiz.a: Correctness is fine: the database is the source of truth and every read becomes a miss. But every read now hits the database, which may not survive the load.

mcq.q: In look-aside caching, what does the application do after writing to the database?
options: Deletes the cache entry so the next reader refills it
Writes the new value into the cache
Waits for the cache to pull the change itself
Leaves the cache alone until the TTL expires
mcq.why: Look-aside deletes on write. The next reader misses, reads the database and fills the current value.

hook: Two writers update the same row. The database ends up right. The cache ends up wrong for good. How?
title: Delete the cache entry on write. Never update it.
body:
Writer A sets a row to 1, then writer B sets it to 2. The database says 2. If each writer also pushes its value into the cache, delays can deliver B's update first and A's second. The cache now says 1, and nothing will fix it.

Deleting avoids this. A **delete** has nothing to reorder, and it is **idempotent**: doing it twice is harmless. The next reader misses and refills with whatever the database holds now.
takeaway: Tell the cache to forget, not what to remember.
deeper:
**Order stops mattering:** With delete-on-write, both writers send a delete. Whichever lands first, the entry is gone, and the next reader reads 2 from the database. A duplicated or retried delete does no harm, which makes deletes safe to retry and to broadcast from a log. Meta's memcache design uses exactly this rule.

**What it does not fix:** A slow reader can still fill an old value after the delete. That is the stale-set race, and Meta's leases exist to close it.

**The price:** Every write causes at least one future miss, because the entry is gone until someone reads it again. For read-heavy workloads that is a good trade, which is why look-aside with delete-on-write is the dominant pattern at scale.

**The quotable version:** Updating tells the cache what to believe. Deleting tells it to go ask the database.

quiz.q: Your invalidation pipeline sometimes delivers the same message twice and occasionally out of order. Why does that matter much less if the messages are deletes rather than new values?
quiz.a: Deletes are idempotent and carry no value to reorder: any delivery order leaves the key empty, and the next reader refills from the database. Out-of-order updates can leave an old value cached.

mcq.q: What is the main advantage of deleting a cache entry on write rather than updating it?
options: Deletes are idempotent and cannot be applied in the wrong order
Deletes are smaller to send over the network than values
Deletes keep the cache warm with no future misses
Deletes stop slow readers from filling stale values
mcq.why: Repeating a delete is harmless and there's no value to reorder, so concurrent writers can't leave an older value cached.

hook: Every team writes its own cache-miss logic, and one will get it wrong. Where should that logic live instead?
title: Read-through: the cache itself fetches on a miss
body: With look-aside, every service writes its own check, miss, read, fill and delete, and every service can get it wrong. In **read-through** caching, the cache itself loads from the database on a miss. The application only ever talks to the cache. The logic lives in one place, but the cache must know how to query the database. Staleness and data-loss risk match look-aside, since the database is still the truth. Uber's CacheFront is an integrated cache of this kind.
takeaway: Centralize the miss path once, and every team inherits the fixes.
deeper:
**Why centralize:** One component owning the miss path means protections get built once for everyone: stale-fill guards, negative caching, invalidation from a log. With look-aside, each team would need to rediscover each one.

**The cost is coupling:** A generic key-value cache like memcached knows nothing about schemas. To read through, the cache must understand how a key maps to a query. That coupling makes read-through a natural fit inside a database platform, as CacheFront shows.

**What it looks like:** Uber's CacheFront sits inside Docstore's query engine. The engine checks Redis, returns cached rows, fetches the rest from storage and fills Redis asynchronously. Write cost is the same as look-aside, a database write plus a delete, and data-loss risk is none.

quiz.q: You want stale-fill protection and negative caching in every service at your company. Why is that far easier with a read-through cache than with look-aside?
quiz.a: In read-through, one component owns the miss path, so you add each protection once. With look-aside, every application implements its own logic and each would need changing.

mcq.q: What does read-through caching require that look-aside does not?
options: The cache must know how to query the database
The application must delete keys after every write
The cache must acknowledge writes before the database
The database must push every change into the cache
mcq.why: In read-through, the cache itself loads missing data, so it must understand how a key maps to a database query.

hook: One cache pattern guarantees a key is fresh the moment it's written. Why isn't it everyone's default?
title: Write-through: always fresh, but every write pays twice
body:
In **write-through** caching, writes go to the cache, and the cache synchronously writes the database before acknowledging. A key you just wrote is always fresh in the cache, and nothing is lost if the cache fails, because the database already has it.

The bill: every write waits for both the cache and the database. And every written key takes cache memory, whether anyone reads it or not. It fits small, hot data like configs and sessions.
takeaway: Write-through pays for freshness on every write, even for data nobody reads.
deeper:
**What it fixes:** After a write, readers of that key see the new value immediately. There is no window where an old value lingers, so staleness risk is low for written keys and data-loss risk is none.

**Cost one, latency:** Acknowledgment waits for the cache write and the database write, so write latency is the sum of both.

**Cost two, memory:** Every written key lands in cache memory. On write-heavy, read-rarely data that wastes space and can evict hot keys that were saving the database real work.

**The catch:** Freshness covers only keys written through the cache. A row changed by some other path, like a job writing the database directly, can still be stale. That is why write-through suits small, hot data such as configuration values and sessions, while look-aside handles large datasets.

quiz.q: A logging service writes millions of events a minute and almost never reads them back. Someone proposes a write-through cache in front of it. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Every write pays cache plus database latency, and every event occupies cache memory though it is never read, wasting memory and possibly evicting hot keys.

mcq.q: What is write-through caching's main weakness?
options: Every write pays both cache and database latency
Acknowledged writes can be lost if the cache dies
Readers see stale values right after a write
The cache must know how to query the database
mcq.why: The cache writes the database synchronously before acknowledging, so each write waits for both.

hook: Which cache pattern can lose data the app was told was saved, and why do big companies still use it?
title: Write-back: fastest writes, until a node dies
body:
In **write-back** (write-behind) caching, writes go to the cache and are acknowledged at once. The cache writes the database later, in batches. That gives the fastest writes of any pattern.

It also breaks the rule that makes caches safe. Between acknowledgment and flush, the cache is the only holder of the data. If the node dies before flushing, those writes are gone. At big-tech scale it is used for counters and metrics that tolerate small loss, never for user data of record.
takeaway: Write-back makes the cache the source of truth until the flush.
deeper:
**Why anyone uses it:** Batching lets many increments to the same counter collapse into one database write, and the client never waits for the database. For a like counter or a metrics buffer, that absorbs a huge write rate cheaply.

**Where it's acceptable:** Only when losing the most recent writes on a cache failure is acceptable. Approximate counters and metrics qualify. A user's profile or a payment never does.

**The rule it breaks:** Every other pattern keeps the database as the truth, so the cache can lose anything. Write-back hands that role to the cache for a window. A crash, a restart or an eviction bug in that window destroys acknowledged writes.

**The scorecard:** Write cost lowest, staleness low, data-loss risk yes on cache failure. Typical uses: counters, metrics, buffers.

quiz.q: A product manager wants write-back caching for checkout orders to cut latency. What do you tell them?
quiz.a: No. Write-back acknowledges before the database has the write, so a cache node dying before its flush loses confirmed orders. It is only for loss-tolerant data like approximate counters or metrics.

mcq.q: Which data is an acceptable fit for write-back caching?
options: Approximate view counters that can lose a few increments
User account balances after each payment
Profile edits that users expect to persist
Order confirmations sent to customers
mcq.why: Write-back can lose recent writes if a node dies before flushing, so only loss-tolerant data like approximate counters belongs there.

hook: Look-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back. Two questions sort them all. Which two?
title: Four cache patterns, sorted by who fills and who writes
body: Two questions sort the four classic patterns: who fills the cache, and when does the database get the write? Look-aside: the app fills on a miss, as in most web caches and memcache at Meta. Read-through: the cache fills on a miss, as in Uber's CacheFront. Write-through: the cache writes the database synchronously, for small hot configs and sessions. **Write-back**: the cache flushes later, for counters, metrics and buffers, and is the only one that can lose data.
takeaway: Move toward write-back and you trade durability for write speed.
deeper:
**Staleness:** Look-aside and read-through both suffer races between a fill and a delete. Write-through keeps written keys fresh. Write-back is low too, since the cache holds the newest value.

**Data loss:** Look-aside, read-through and write-through have none, because the database remains the truth. Write-back loses whatever had not flushed when the cache fails.

**Write cost:** Look-aside and read-through pay a database write plus a delete. Write-through is higher, since each write waits for both systems. Write-back is lowest.

**Where big tech lands:** Look-aside or read-through with delete-on-write for data of record, plus commit-log invalidation and a TTL as safety net. Write-back only for data that tolerates small loss. Write-through where a small set of keys must be fresh right after writes and write latency is acceptable.

quiz.q: You need a cache for (a) session data that must be fresh right after login, and (b) page-view counters absorbing huge write rates. Which pattern fits each?
quiz.a: Sessions: write-through, fresh for written keys with no loss risk. Counters: write-back, lowest write cost, and losing a few increments on cache failure is acceptable.

mcq.q: Which cache pattern is the only one with data-loss risk on cache failure?
options: Write-back
Write-through
Read-through
Look-aside
mcq.why: Write-back acknowledges before the database has the write; if the node dies before flushing, the write is gone.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: Every client followed the rules exactly. The cache still holds old data with no expiry in sight. How?
title: The stale set: a paused reader poisons the cache
body: Reader A misses and reads the old value from the database. Then it pauses, say for garbage collection. Writer B updates the database and deletes the cache key. A wakes up and sets the old value into the cache. The delete already happened, so nothing removes it: stale data with no expiry in sight. Meta's memcache paper calls this a **stale set**.
takeaway: A delete can only remove what's already there. The stale set arrives after.
deeper:
**Nobody did anything wrong:** The reader followed look-aside exactly. The writer wrote the database and then deleted the key. The failure is ordering: the delete landed in the gap between the reader's database read and its cache fill, removed nothing, and the fill resurrected old data.

**How long it lives:** Until something evicts it or a TTL expires it. With no TTL, effectively forever. That is why a TTL belongs on every entry even when you also invalidate.

**The fixes:** Both let the cache notice that a fill is older than something that already happened. Meta's leases give each miss a token that a later delete invalidates, so the late set is rejected. Uber's CacheFront runs Lua scripts in Redis that compare timestamps, so a late fill cannot overwrite fresher data.

**The joke is earned:** Phil Karlton said the two hard things in computer science are cache invalidation and naming things.

quiz.q: Your cache runs correct look-aside code, yet a profile shows a week-old name and no TTL is set. GC logs show a long pause on one web server around the last edit. What happened?
quiz.a: A stale set: that server read the old row, paused, and after the writer's delete it filled the old value. With no TTL, it never expires.

mcq.q: In the stale-set race, why doesn't the writer's delete clean up the stale value?
options: The delete runs before the slow reader fills the old value
The delete is sent over UDP and gets dropped
The delete goes to a replica instead of the primary
The delete is rejected because the key has a TTL
mcq.why: The reader fills after the delete already ran, so there was nothing to delete then and nothing deletes it afterward.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: The delete was correct and on time. The cache still refilled with old data a moment later. From where?
title: Replication lag: the cache refills from a stale replica
body:
The app writes the primary database in one region and deletes the cache key. A reader in another region misses and reads its local **replica**, which has not received the write yet. It fills the cache with the old value.

The invalidation worked. The source used to refill was itself behind. This race appears whenever writes go to a primary and reads go to asynchronous replicas, the normal multi-region setup.
takeaway: A cache is only as fresh as whatever it refills from.
deeper:
**Meta's setup:** One region holds the primary databases and the others hold replicas, so this race is built in.

**Fix one, travel with the data:** McSqueal's invalidations flow with MySQL replication, so a replica region's cache deletes arrive alongside the data change rather than racing ahead of it.

**Fix two, remote markers:** When a web server in a non-primary region writes, it sets a marker in the regional cache, writes to the primary region's database, and deletes the local key. A later reader that sees the marker knows the local replica may be behind and reads from the primary region instead.

**The catch:** Timing the delete perfectly is not enough. If the refill source lags, a well-timed delete just makes room for old data.

quiz.q: A user in Europe edits their bio; the primary database is in the US. The European cache key is deleted immediately, yet their reload shows the old bio. Why?
quiz.a: The reload missed and refilled from the European replica, which had not yet received the write. The delete worked; the refill source was stale.

mcq.q: What makes the replication-lag race different from the stale-set race?
options: The refill reads from a replica that hasn't received the write
The delete is lost when the app server crashes
Two writers update the cache in the wrong order
A paused reader fills a value it read before the write
mcq.why: The delete succeeds; the problem is that the next fill comes from a lagging replica still holding the old value.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: The database has the new value. The cache has the old one. Nothing in your code will retry. What happened?
title: Lost invalidations: the delete that never arrives
body:
The app writes the database, then crashes before sending the delete. Or it sends the delete over a network that drops it. Either way, the database holds the new value, the cache keeps serving the old one, and nothing will retry.

Any design that trusts application code to deliver every delete will leak stale entries eventually. The fix is to invalidate from the database's **commit log**, which is durable and ordered, instead of from the app.
takeaway: If the app sends the invalidation, the invalidation can die with the app.
deeper:
**Move it to the log:** Meta runs McSqueal on every database. It reads committed SQL statements, extracts the cache keys to invalidate, and broadcasts deletes. Uber's CacheFront uses Flux, which tails the MySQL binlog.

**Why the log is safe:** It is durable and ordered. An app server crash cannot lose an invalidation, and after a failure the deletes can be replayed. Every committed write is in the log, so every committed write eventually produces its delete.

**The backstop:** Even log-driven invalidation can miss: a bug in key extraction, a write path that skips the normal flow. A TTL catches what slips through. A missed invalidation with no TTL lives forever.

**The common mistake:** Invalidating on write does not make a cache consistent unless all three races are handled.

quiz.q: Your app deletes cache keys right after each database commit. During a deploy, hundreds of servers are killed mid-request. What stale-data risk did the deploy create, and what design removes it?
quiz.a: Some servers committed writes but died before sending deletes, leaving stale entries. Invalidating from the database commit log (like McSqueal or Flux) removes it, since the log survives crashes and can be replayed.

mcq.q: Why can't an invalidation be lost when deletes come from the commit log?
options: The log is durable and ordered, so deletes survive crashes and replay
The log sends every delete twice over separate networks
The log blocks writes until every cache confirms the delete
The log stores deletes in the cache before the write commits
mcq.why: Every committed write is in the durable log, so its invalidation can't vanish with a crashed app server and can be replayed.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: A TTL doesn't stop a single stale read. So why is 'always set one' among the firmest rules in caching?
title: Always set a TTL: it bounds staleness you didn't prevent
body:
A **TTL** (time to live) makes every entry expire after a set time. It does not prevent staleness: a wrong value still serves until it expires. What it does is bound it. Whatever race or bug left an entry wrong, it cannot stay wrong longer than the TTL.

So set a TTL even when you invalidate on write or from a commit log. Invalidation handles the normal case. The TTL is the safety net for bugs.
takeaway: Invalidation keeps you fresh. A TTL keeps you from being wrong forever.
deeper:
**Two layers, two jobs:** Commit-log invalidation keeps the cache fresh soon after a write. The TTL guarantees an upper bound when invalidation fails: a stale set, a lost delete, a refill from a lagging replica, or a write path nobody hooked up.

**Without it:** A missed invalidation with no TTL lives forever.

**The knock-on effects:** Shorter TTLs mean less staleness but more misses and more database load. Keys written together with the same TTL expire together and cause a stampede, which is why TTLs get jitter, for example 1 hour plus or minus 10 minutes.

**Where TTLs run short:** In-process caches for hot keys use TTLs of seconds, because those copies usually get no invalidations. Meta's Gutter pool entries also expire quickly.

quiz.q: Your team invalidates from the binlog and wants to drop TTLs to push hit ratio higher. What's the risk?
quiz.a: Any invalidation that slips through, from a stale set, replica refill or key-extraction bug, would stay wrong forever. The TTL is the only thing bounding those failures.

mcq.q: What does a TTL guarantee about stale cache entries?
options: They cannot stay stale longer than the TTL
They are never served after a write
They are replaced by the next writer
They are detected and logged by the cache
mcq.why: A TTL doesn't stop a stale value from serving, but every entry expires, so staleness has an upper bound.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: What if no application code ever had to remember which cache keys to delete?
title: McSqueal and Flux: invalidate from the commit log
body: Asking every write path to remember its cache deletes fails eventually. So Meta runs a daemon called **McSqueal** on every database. It reads committed SQL statements, extracts the cache keys to invalidate, and broadcasts deletes to every frontend cluster in the region. Uber's CacheFront does the same with **Flux**, which tails the MySQL binlog. The log is durable and ordered, so invalidations survive app crashes and can be replayed.
takeaway: Derive invalidations from what committed, not from what the app remembered.
deeper:
**The path:**
1. Web servers send SQL writes to the MySQL primary.
2. The primary records them in its commit log or binlog.
3. The daemon reads the log and sends batched deletes to a cache router per cluster, such as mcrouter.
4. The router forwards them to the cache servers, while web servers keep doing get and fill on miss.

**Correctness leaves the app:** A team adding a new write path no longer needs to know which keys to delete, as long as the daemon can derive keys from the committed change. At Meta, these invalidations also flow with MySQL replication to other regions.

**Not the whole story:** Flux invalidates or updates Redis within seconds, and Uber's write path also invalidates directly for fresher reads. Log-driven invalidation alone does not stop a late fill, so CacheFront adds Lua timestamp checks.

quiz.q: A new batch job updates rows straight in MySQL, bypassing the app, and its changes leave stale cache entries under app-sent invalidation. Why would McSqueal-style invalidation not have this problem?
quiz.a: McSqueal reads committed statements from the database's log, so every committed change produces deletes regardless of which code path wrote it.

mcq.q: How does Meta's McSqueal decide which cache keys to delete?
options: It extracts keys from committed SQL statements in the database log
Web servers tell it which keys they changed after each write
It scans the cache for entries older than the database rows
It deletes every key in the region on a fixed schedule
mcq.why: McSqueal runs on each database, reads committed SQL, derives affected cache keys and broadcasts deletes to the region's frontend clusters.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: A slow reader shows up with old data after fresher data is already cached. How does the cache know to say no?
title: Versioned values: old data can never overwrite new
body: Late fills are the recurring villain: a slow reader arrives with old data after fresher data is already cached. **Versioning** stops them. Store a version or timestamp with each cached value, and refuse to overwrite a newer value with an older one. Uber's CacheFront does this with Lua scripts inside Redis that compare row timestamps. Because the check runs inside the cache, the compare and the write happen as one atomic step.
takeaway: Let the newer value win, no matter which one arrives last.
deeper:
**Why inside Redis:** A compare-then-set from the application has its own race. Two clients each read the current version, each decide theirs is newer, and both write. A Lua script executes atomically on the Redis server, so nothing can interleave between the compare and the write.

**Where it fits:** Log-driven invalidation keeps the cache fresh and makes deletes unlosable. A TTL bounds anything that slips through. Versioning handles ordering: whenever two cache writes race, the newer data wins regardless of arrival order. Meta's leases solve a similar problem differently, by invalidating a filler's token when a delete arrives.

**Read-your-writes:** Versioned values are one way to give users their own writes back. A client that knows the version it just wrote can recognize an older cached value. The alternative is routing that user's reads to the database for a short time after they write.

quiz.q: Two cache fills for the same row race: one carries a newer timestamp, the other an older one, and the older fill arrives last. With versioned values, what's cached, and why must the check run inside Redis?
quiz.a: The newer value stays, since older can't overwrite newer. The check runs as an atomic Lua script so no other fill can slip in between the compare and the write.

mcq.q: Why does CacheFront compare timestamps in a Redis Lua script rather than in application code?
options: The script runs atomically, so no fill can interleave between compare and write
Lua scripts run faster than any application language
Application servers cannot read timestamps stored in Redis
Redis rejects writes that do not come from a script
mcq.why: An app-side compare-then-set lets two clients both decide they're newer; an atomic server-side script makes compare and write one step.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: You save your profile far from the primary database, reload, and the edit seems gone. What stops that?
title: Remote markers: read-after-write for far-away users
body:
At Meta, one region holds the primary databases and others hold replicas. A user in a replica region who saves and reloads would miss, read the lagging local replica, and cache the old profile again.

**Remote markers** fix it. The writing web server first sets a marker in the regional cache, then writes to the primary region's database, then deletes the local key. A reader that sees the marker skips the local replica and reads from the primary region.
takeaway: Pay for the cross-region read only on keys that were just written.
deeper:
**Why a marker works:** It is a small, cheap signal stored in the fast cache layer. It turns a region-wide consistency problem into a per-key decision. Most reads keep using the local replica. Only keys with a recent remote write pay for a cross-region read.

**The order matters:**
1. Set the marker in the regional cache.
2. Write to the primary region's database.
3. Delete the local cache key.
A reader arriving after step 3 misses, sees the marker, and goes to the primary instead of the replica.

**The general rule:** If a feature needs read-your-writes, route that user's reads to the database or primary for a short time after they write, or use versioned values. Remote markers are one production implementation of that routing.

quiz.q: Why would it be wasteful to route every read in a replica region to the primary region, and how do remote markers avoid that?
quiz.a: Most keys weren't just written, so the local replica is fine and cross-region reads only add latency. Markers flag only recently written keys, so only those reads go to the primary.

mcq.q: What does a reader in a Meta replica region do when it finds a remote marker for a key?
options: Reads the value from the primary region's database
Waits until the marker's TTL expires, then retries
Reads the local replica and refreshes the marker
Returns the cached value and ignores the replica
mcq.why: The marker signals a recent remote write the local replica may lack, so the reader goes to the primary region instead.

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: Meta counted how many of its cache deletes actually removed something, and what all of them cost the network.
title: Only 4% of Meta's cache deletes hit anything
body:
A write invalidates every key that might depend on it, cached or not. At Meta, only 4 percent of deletes hit cached data. Yet sending every delete straight from every database to every cache server made packet rates too high.

The fix was **batching**. McSqueal packs deletes together and sends them to a few mcrouter servers per cluster, which fan them out. The median deletes per packet improved 18 times.

stat.label: better median deletes per packet from batching

takeaway: At scale, the invalidation stream is traffic you must engineer, not a free side effect.
deeper:
**Why so few hit:** A cache holds only what was recently read. A log-driven invalidator cannot cheaply know which keys are present, so it sends deletes for everything a write might affect. Most are no-ops. Deletes being idempotent makes that safe.

**The real cost is packets:** With many databases and many cache servers, an all-to-all stream means a flood of tiny packets, each carrying almost nothing.

**Changing the topology:** Databases talk to a handful of mcrouter servers per cluster. Those routers pack many deletes into each packet and fan them out locally. That raised the median deletes per packet 18 times.

**The lesson:** Correctness was never the problem here. Throughput of the correctness machinery was.

quiz.q: Your commit-log invalidator sends each delete directly from every database to every cache server, and most deletes hit nothing. Packet rates are exploding. What did Meta do in the same spot?
quiz.a: Batch deletes and send them to a few mcrouter servers per cluster, which fan them out. That raised median deletes per packet by 18 times.

mcq.q: Why could Meta safely send so many deletes that removed nothing?
options: Deletes are idempotent, so a delete for an absent key is harmless
Cache servers queue deletes until the key is next read
Each delete carried a version that prevented duplicates
Deletes went over UDP, so extra ones cost nothing
mcq.why: Deleting a key that isn't cached, or deleting twice, changes nothing, so over-sending is only a network cost, not a correctness risk.

predict.q: What share of Meta's cache invalidations actually hit cached data?
options: About 4 percent
About 40 percent
About 80 percent

section: 6.3 Invalidation and consistency: the hard part
hook: A user changes their name and the old one comes back. The code deletes the key on every write. How?
title: Delete-on-write doesn't make a cache consistent
body: The bug report says: 'I changed my name and the old one came back.' The team sees the delete right after the write and concludes the cache is fine. But delete-on-write closes only one gap. A slow reader can fill old data after the delete. A reader in another region can refill from a lagging replica. A crash can skip the delete entirely. Look-aside with delete-on-write is **eventually consistent**, not strongly consistent.
takeaway: Deleting on write shrinks the stale window. It doesn't close it.
deeper:
**Decide per feature:** Most reads, like friend counts or post counters, tolerate a few seconds of staleness. Some, like a user seeing their own just-saved edit, need read-your-writes.

**For read-your-writes:** Route that user's reads to the database for a short time after they write; Meta's remote markers apply the same idea per key across regions. Or use versioned values so an older cached value can be recognized.

**Close each race by name:**
1. Stale sets: leases or timestamp checks reject late fills.
2. Lost deletes: invalidate from the commit log.
3. Replica refills: markers or primary reads after a write.
4. Everything else: a TTL bounds it.

**The catch:** None of these make look-aside strongly consistent. They make staleness rare, short-lived and bounded by design.

quiz.q: A spec says 'after a user edits a post, they must see the edit immediately.' Your stack is look-aside memcache with delete-on-write. Is that enough, and if not, what do you add?
quiz.a: No; delete-on-write is eventually consistent. Route that user's reads to the database briefly after they write, or use versioned values so older cached data is recognized.

mcq.q: What consistency does look-aside caching with delete-on-write provide?
options: Eventual consistency
Strong consistency
Linearizable reads
Read-your-writes by default
mcq.why: Races like stale sets, replica refills and lost deletes can briefly or lastingly serve old data, so the cache only converges eventually.

hook: One popular key expires. Seconds later the database is drowning. What turned one miss into thousands?
title: Thundering herd: one missing key, thousands of DB hits
body: A **thundering herd**, or cache stampede, starts when a popular key disappears: expiry, invalidation, eviction or a restart. Thousands of requests miss at the same moment, and all of them go to the database for the same row. The database slows, requests time out, clients retry, and load climbs further. Every one of those requests also wants to fill the cache, so the key stays empty until one of them finishes.
takeaway: The more popular the key, the bigger the crowd waiting when it vanishes.
deeper:
**A feedback loop:**
1. The first wave of misses adds load.
2. Load raises database latency.
3. Latency causes timeouts.
4. Timeouts cause retries, which add more load.

**Why popular keys are dangerous:** The more requests per second a key receives, the more pile up during the time it takes to refill it. And databases are provisioned for peak load, so herd spikes drive hardware cost directly.

**The defenses:** Meta's leases let one client refill a key while others wait. Request coalescing merges concurrent misses inside one process or proxy. Jittered TTLs stop keys written together from expiring together. Early refresh renews hot keys before they expire. Serving stale on error avoids hitting an overloaded database at all. Capped retries with backoff break the retry spiral.

quiz.q: A viral post's cache entry expires at peak. Database latency rises and query volume keeps climbing even though user traffic is flat. Explain the extra volume.
quiz.a: A thundering herd: thousands of simultaneous misses hit the database and slow it; timeouts trigger retries that add more queries, while the key stays unfilled until one request completes.

mcq.q: Which event can start a thundering herd on a popular key?
options: The key expires and many requests miss at once
The key is read by many clients while cached
The key is written to the database by one user
The key is copied to a replica in another zone
mcq.why: When a popular key disappears, every concurrent request misses together and sends the same query to the database.

hook: How do you stop a slow reader from writing old data into the cache, without asking the database for versions?
title: Leases: a 64-bit token that kills the stale set
body: Meta's **leases** (2013) fix the stale set with one small mechanism. On a miss, memcached hands the client a 64-bit token tied to that key. The client reads the database and sets the value along with the token. If a delete for that key arrived in the meantime, memcached has already invalidated the token, so the set is rejected. The slow reader can no longer resurrect old data.
takeaway: The token means 'nothing changed since you asked.' A delete revokes it.
deeper:
**Replay the race with leases:**
1. Reader A misses and receives token T for key K.
2. A reads the old value, then pauses.
3. Writer B updates the database and deletes K; memcached invalidates T.
4. A wakes and tries to set K with T. Memcached rejects it.
5. The next reader misses, gets a fresh token, and fills the current value.

**The elegance:** The cache itself detects the ordering problem. The application needs no versions or timestamps from the database.

**A bonus option:** Recently deleted items are kept briefly, and a client that can tolerate staleness gets the old value instead of waiting for a fresh fill.

**The alternative:** Uber's CacheFront blocks the same stale fill with timestamp comparisons in Redis Lua scripts.

quiz.q: With leases on, reader A holds a token for key K and is paused. A writer updates the row and deletes K. A resumes and sets K. What happens, and what does the next reader do?
quiz.a: A's set is rejected, because the delete invalidated its token. The next reader misses, gets a fresh token, and fills the current value from the database.

mcq.q: What causes memcached to reject a set that carries a lease token?
options: A delete for that key arrived after the token was issued
The token is older than the key's configured TTL
Another client already holds a token for the same key
The value is larger than the token allows
mcq.why: A delete invalidates outstanding tokens for the key, so a fill based on a pre-delete database read is refused.

hook: Herd-prone keys pushed Meta's database to 17,000 queries/sec at peak. One small rule fixed it. What rule?
title: Leases cut herd peaks from 17,000 to 1,300 queries/sec
body: Leases double as herd control. Memcached hands out a **lease token** for a given key at most once every 10 seconds. Every other client that misses in that window gets a 'wait and retry shortly' response instead of going to the database. By the time they retry, the lease holder has usually filled the value, so they hit. For keys prone to herds, Meta's peak database query rate fell from 17,000 per second to 1,300.
takeaway: Let one client fetch; make the crowd wait in the cache.
deeper:
**Without leases:** Every client that misses a hot key goes to the database, so a key taking thousands of requests per second sends thousands of identical queries.

**With leases:** One client per key per 10-second window is allowed to fetch. Everyone else pauses briefly and reads the freshly filled value from the cache.

**Why peak is the number:** Databases are provisioned for peak load, so dropping peak queries from 17,000 to 1,300 per second is a direct hardware saving, not a nicer average.

**Two problems, one mechanism:** The token check blocks stale sets, and the limit on issuing tokens collapses a herd into a single database read. Clients that accept slightly stale data can skip even the wait: recently deleted items are kept briefly and served to them.

quiz.q: A hot key expires and 5,000 clients miss within the same second. With Meta-style leases, roughly how many go to the database, and what do the rest do?
quiz.a: About one: memcached issues a lease for that key at most once every 10 seconds. The others get 'wait and retry shortly' and usually hit once the holder fills the value.

mcq.q: How often does memcached issue a lease token for the same key, to limit herds?
options: At most once every 10 seconds
At most once every second
At most once every 60 seconds
Once per client per key
mcq.why: Limiting tokens to one per key per 10 seconds lets a single client refill while the others wait and retry.

predict.q: Meta throttled refills of herd-prone keys with leases. Peak database queries were 17,000 per second before. After?
options: 1,300 per second
8,500 per second
14,000 per second

hook: A hundred threads in one process miss the same key at once. How many database queries should that cost?
title: Single-flight: many identical misses, one backend call
body: **Request coalescing**, also called single-flight, works inside one process or proxy. When several concurrent requests miss on the same key, only one backend call goes out. The others wait and share its result. A hundred threads querying the same row becomes one query and a hundred answers. It needs no coordination with the cache server, just a local table of keys with a request already in flight.
takeaway: If the question is already in flight, wait for the answer. Don't ask again.
deeper:
**Local versus fleet-wide:** Leases coordinate at the cache server, across every client. Coalescing works inside a single process or proxy: new requests for an in-flight key attach to the existing call instead of starting another.

**Its strength:** Simple, no extra round trip, and it helps even when the backend is not a cache at all.

**Its limit:** With thousands of web servers, each process still sends its own query, so the database can see one request per process. That is often good enough, and it pairs well with leases for the rest.

**Where it sits in a crisis:** When a hit-ratio drop drives database latency and timeouts up, request coalescing, leases and load shedding are the mitigations that shield the database.

quiz.q: You add single-flight to each of your 2,000 web servers. A hot key expires. What's the worst-case number of database queries for that key now, and what would cut it further?
quiz.a: About 2,000, one per process, since coalescing only merges misses within a process. Leases at the cache server can cut it to roughly one across the fleet.

mcq.q: What limits request coalescing compared with Meta's leases?
options: It only merges misses within one process or proxy
It requires the database to support batched queries
It only works for keys that have a TTL set
It needs a round trip to the cache server first
mcq.why: Coalescing is local bookkeeping, so each process in a large fleet can still send one query; leases coordinate across all clients.

hook: A batch job loads a million keys with a 1-hour TTL. Exactly one hour later, the database spikes. Why?
title: Jitter your TTLs so keys don't all expire at once
body:
Caches often fill in bursts: after a deploy, a warmup or a batch job. Give those keys the same TTL and they all expire at the same instant one TTL later, sending a synchronized wave of misses to the database. It is a thundering herd across many keys instead of one.

**Jittered TTLs** add randomness: instead of exactly 1 hour, use 1 hour plus or minus 10 minutes. The spike becomes a trickle.
takeaway: Keys born together die together, unless you randomize their lifespans.
deeper:
**The repeat problem:** With a fixed TTL, a burst-filled set of keys ages out together, refills together, and ages out together again. The miss wave recurs every TTL period. A cache that refilled in a rush after a restart carries the same hidden timer.

**What jitter does:** A random offset per key spreads expiries across a window, 20 minutes wide in the example, instead of one instant. That lowers peak database load, the number that drives provisioning.

**Why it's cheap:** Only the TTL calculation changes. No coordination, no extra infrastructure.

**How the defenses divide the work:** Leases and coalescing handle many requests for one key. Jitter handles many keys expiring together. Early refresh keeps the hottest keys from expiring at all while they are in demand.

quiz.q: After a deploy, your cache refills every key in one burst, all with a 30-minute TTL. What pattern will database load show, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: A sharp miss spike every 30 minutes as the keys expire together and refill together. Add random jitter to each TTL so expiries spread out.

mcq.q: What problem do jittered TTLs solve?
options: Many keys written together expiring at the same moment
One very hot key overloading a single shard
A slow reader filling stale data after a delete
A delete being lost when the app server crashes
mcq.why: Randomizing each key's TTL spreads expiries over a window, so a burst of keys doesn't miss all at once.

hook: The database is overloaded and a hot key just expired. Failing makes it worse. What else can the cache do?
title: Refresh early, and serve stale when the database struggles
body: Two techniques keep a hot key available while its value is renewed. **Early refresh** reloads the key in the background shortly before it expires, so readers never see a miss. Making it probabilistic means only some requests near expiry trigger it. **Serve stale on error** returns the expired value when the database is overloaded instead of failing. Both trade a little freshness for availability.
takeaway: A slightly old answer beats piling more load onto a drowning database.
deeper:
**Attack the root cause:** Expiry herds happen because the key disappears. If a background refresh replaces the value just before the TTL ends, there is never a gap, so there is no miss wave. The probabilistic trigger stops every request near expiry from launching its own refresh.

**A degradation mode:** Normally, expired values are not served. When the database is overloaded, returning a slightly old value keeps the product working and, crucially, adds no load to a database that is already struggling. Meta's leases offer something similar: recently deleted items are kept briefly and handed to clients that can tolerate staleness.

**The boundary:** Both only suit data where brief staleness is fine, like counters, feeds or profiles. For read-your-writes, route reads to the database after a write or use versioned values.

quiz.q: Your cache layer serves stale on error. During a database overload, is that a good trade for (a) a product's view count and (b) a user's just-updated shipping address?
quiz.a: Yes for view counts, where brief staleness is harmless and it sheds load. No for the address, which needs read-your-writes; route that user's reads to the database or use versioned values.

mcq.q: How does early probabilistic refresh prevent a stampede on a hot key?
options: It reloads the key before expiry, so the key never goes missing
It extends the key's TTL each time the key is read
It blocks all readers until the refreshed value arrives
It copies the key to several shards before it expires
mcq.why: Refreshing in the background just before the TTL ends means readers never find the key missing, so no miss wave forms.

hook: You double your cache servers. One of them stays pinned at full load. Why didn't more shards help?
title: A hot key lives on one shard, so sharding can't save you
body: A **hot key** is one key taking a huge share of traffic: a celebrity's profile, a viral post, a global config value. Sharding spreads different keys across servers. It cannot split the load of one key, because each key lives on exactly one shard. Meta noted that a single key can account for 20 percent of a server's requests. That server saturates while the rest of the cluster idles.
takeaway: Sharding balances many keys. It does nothing for one.
deeper:
**Why partitioning fails here:** Consistent hashing and hash slots map each key to exactly one owner. That balances load when traffic spreads over many keys of similar popularity. If one key alone exceeds what a server can handle, no resharding helps. The key has to land somewhere.

**It makes failures worse:** If the server holding a hot key dies and its keys rehash onto survivors, the hot key can overload the next server, which dies, and so on. Meta's Gutter pool exists partly to stop that cascade.

**The fixes change where reads are served:**
1. Replicate hot keys across several servers.
2. Cache the hottest keys in-process with a short TTL.
3. Split a key into several named copies.
4. Detect hot keys by sampling per-key traffic in the cache proxy.

quiz.q: A global feature-flag key is read on every request, and its cache shard runs hot while others idle. A teammate proposes moving to 4× more shards. Why won't that work, and what would?
quiz.a: The key still maps to one shard, so its load doesn't move. Replicate it across servers, cache it in-process with a seconds-long TTL, or split it into several copies.

mcq.q: Why doesn't adding cache shards fix a hot key?
options: Each key maps to exactly one shard, however many exist
More shards increase the hot key's replication lag
Consistent hashing sends new shards only cold keys
Hot keys are pinned to the oldest shard in the ring
mcq.why: Sharding divides keys, not a key's traffic, so all requests for the hot key still land on one server.

predict.q: Meta measured how much of one cache server's requests a single key can take. Up to what share?
options: 20 percent
2 percent
0.2 percent

hook: One key needs more reads per second than any single server can give. Where does the extra capacity come from?
title: Replicate hot keys and spread reads across the copies
body: If one server can't absorb a key's reads, put the key on several servers and spread reads across the copies. Meta uses **replicated pools**: a set of keys stored in full on multiple servers, so any replica can answer. Netflix EVCache keeps a full copy of its data in each availability zone and reads from the local zone. Instead of one server taking a hot key's entire read rate, the load divides across every copy.
takeaway: No partition fixes a hot key; only more copies or closer copies do.
deeper:
**The trade:** Replication buys read capacity with memory and write work. Every extra copy costs memory, and every write or invalidation must reach every copy. So Meta applies it selectively: keys that benefit go into a replicated pool rather than duplicating everything.

**EVCache goes broad for other reasons:** A full copy per zone keeps reads local, cutting latency and cross-zone traffic. An item missing locally, from instance failure or eviction, can be read from another zone. Writes go to all zones. Hot keys get spread across zones as a side effect.

**The principle:** No partitioning scheme fixes a hot key, so the design must replicate its reads or move them closer to the client. Replication is the first half. In-process caching with a short TTL is the second.

quiz.q: You replicate a hot key onto 5 cache servers. Reads are fine now, but an edit to that key sometimes shows old data. What did replication add to the write path that you may have missed?
quiz.a: Every write or invalidation must reach all 5 copies. If one delete misses a copy, readers routed there see the old value until it's fixed or expires.

mcq.q: What does replicating a hot key across several cache servers cost?
options: Extra memory per copy, and every write must reach all copies
Higher read latency, since reads must query every copy
Loss of durability, since copies are acknowledged early
A lease on every read to pick the freshest copy
mcq.why: Copies spread reads but each consumes memory, and each write or invalidation must update every copy.

hook: Thousands of web servers read the same config value on every request. How do you make that nearly free?
title: In-process caches take the hottest keys off the network
body:
For the very hottest keys, the application keeps a local, **in-process cache** with a TTL of seconds. Reads come from the app's own memory with no network call, which takes that load off the network and the cache servers entirely.

The short TTL is essential. A local copy typically receives no invalidations, so the TTL is the only thing bounding how stale it can get. A few seconds of staleness buys huge relief.
takeaway: The fastest cache read is the one that never leaves the process.
deeper:
**The math:** A config value read on every request by thousands of web servers can generate millions of cache reads per second. A local copy refreshed every few seconds turns that into a handful of refreshes per server. The shard owning the key stops being a bottleneck.

**The cost is consistency:** Each process refreshes on its own schedule, so servers can briefly disagree, and a write takes up to one TTL to show everywhere. Fine for configuration, viral post contents or celebrity profiles. Not fine where users need read-your-writes.

**Keep it small:** Local caching uses application memory, so reserve it for the very hottest keys. To find them, sample per-key traffic in the cache proxy and flag keys above a threshold.

quiz.q: You cache a feature flag in-process with a 1-hour TTL to maximize savings. Someone flips the flag off during an incident. What happens, and what should the TTL be?
quiz.a: Servers keep the old value for up to an hour, since local copies get no invalidations. Use a TTL of seconds so the change propagates quickly.

mcq.q: Why must an in-process hot-key cache use a very short TTL?
options: Local copies usually get no invalidations, so the TTL bounds staleness
Application memory is too small to hold keys for long
Short TTLs let the cache server rebalance the key faster
Long TTLs cause the local copy to leak memory over time
mcq.why: Nothing deletes a process's private copy on write, so expiry after a few seconds is what limits how stale it can get.

hook: Your cache can't replicate, but one key is melting a shard. How do you spread it with plain sharding?
title: Key splitting: store key#1 to key#N, read one at random
body:
**Key splitting** spreads a hot key by storing copies under different names, key#1 through key#N. Each name hashes to a different shard, so reads, which pick a random copy, spread across N servers. It is replication built from ordinary sharding.

The catch is on writes. Every write must update or delete all N copies, or readers see different versions depending on which copy they happen to pick.
takeaway: Splitting a key multiplies its read capacity and its write obligations.
deeper:
**Works anywhere:** Because the suffix changes the key, consistent hashing or hash slots scatter the copies across the cluster, and read load for the original key divides by roughly N. The cache servers need no special support.

**Complexity moves to the application:** Writers must know the key is split and how many copies exist, and invalidate all of them. If one delete is lost, one copy stays stale and a fraction of readers see old data. A TTL on each copy bounds that. Changing N later needs care so no copy is orphaned.

**Reserve it for known offenders:** Find candidates with detection, sampling per-key traffic in the cache proxy. At design time, ask for the expected top-1 key rate, not just total rate.

quiz.q: You split a hot key into key#1 through key#8. After an update, about one in eight readers keeps seeing the old value. What most likely went wrong?
quiz.a: One copy's delete or update was lost, so readers who randomly pick that copy get stale data. Writes must reach all N copies; a TTL per copy bounds the damage.

mcq.q: When a hot key is split into key#1 through key#N, what must every write do?
options: Update or delete all N copies
Update only the copy with the highest suffix
Update one random copy and let TTLs sync the rest
Update the original key, which the copies follow
mcq.why: Readers pick a random copy, so any copy left unchanged serves old data to some fraction of readers.

hook: The review approved total QPS with room to spare. At launch, one server fell over. What number was missing?
title: Ask for the top-1 key rate, not just total QPS
body: Total request rate tells you how many servers you need when load spreads evenly. The **top-1 key rate** tells you whether any single server gets overwhelmed, no matter how many you have. Hot keys are the cache version of DynamoDB's single hot item: no partitioning scheme fixes them. So ask for both numbers. If the top key's rate nears one server's capacity, plan replication or client-side caching from day one.
takeaway: Total QPS sizes the fleet. Top-1 key rate sizes the worst server.
deeper:
**Two capacity questions:** Most designs answer only the first. A system can handle its total load comfortably and still fall over because one key exceeds one server.

**Below the line:** If the top-1 rate is well under what one server handles, ordinary sharding works. Near or above it, plan a hot-key strategy up front: replicated pools, per-zone copies, in-process caching with short TTLs, or key splitting.

**For the keys you didn't predict:** A viral post or a sudden celebrity event creates hot keys nobody planned for. A cache proxy already sees every request, so it can sample per-key traffic and flag keys above a threshold. Meta saw a single key reach 20 percent of a server's requests.

**Failure design too:** Meta's Gutter pool exists partly to avoid rehashing a hot key onto a healthy server.

quiz.q: A proposal says: '1 million reads/sec total, 50 cache servers at 50,000 reads/sec each, 2.5× headroom.' The top key gets 80,000 reads/sec. Is the design safe?
quiz.a: No. That key maps to one server, which handles only 50,000 reads/sec, so it overloads regardless of total headroom. Replicate the key or cache it in-process.

mcq.q: Why should a cache design review ask for the expected top-1 key rate?
options: One key maps to one server, so its rate can exceed that server's capacity
The top key determines how much memory the cluster needs
The top key's rate sets the TTL for every other key
The top key decides how many shards consistent hashing creates
mcq.why: Total rate sizes the fleet, but a single key's traffic can't be split by sharding, so it must fit one server or be replicated.

hook: Memcached is little more than get, set and delete. Meta ran it at billions of requests/sec. How?
title: Scaling Memcache: a simple server inside a huge system
body: The NSDI 2013 paper 'Scaling Memcache at Facebook' describes the largest memcached deployment of its time: billions of requests per second and trillions of items. **Memcached** itself is a simple in-memory key-value server with get, set and delete. Meta's contribution is everything around it: routing, networking, pools, failure handling, invalidation and cross-region consistency. A page load can fetch hundreds of keys, so latency depends on fan-out.
takeaway: Keep the server dumb; put the intelligence in the system around it.
deeper:
**Inside a cluster:** Many memcached servers, keys spread by consistent hashing. Gets over UDP, sets and deletes through mcrouter, flow control against incast, pools for different workloads, and a Gutter pool for failures.

**Across clusters in a region:** Several frontend clusters share one storage cluster. Each frontend cluster has its own full cache, plus a shared regional pool for less popular, large items, and Cold Cluster Warmup for new clusters.

**Across regions:** Primary databases in one region, replicas elsewhere. McSqueal invalidations flow alongside MySQL replication, and remote markers protect read-after-write.

**The catch:** Meta calls this a demand-filled look-aside cache, so every look-aside race applies. The paper introduced leases for stale sets and herds. Later, TAO took over many social-graph reads from this layer.

quiz.q: A page at Meta fetches hundreds of keys from different memcached servers. One server is briefly slow. Why does that one server set the whole page's latency?
quiz.a: The page waits for all its keys, so the slowest response among hundreds decides when it can render. With that much fan-out, some slow response is almost always included.

mcq.q: According to Meta's 2013 paper, what did Meta build beyond memcached itself?
options: Routing, pools, failure handling, invalidation and cross-region consistency
A new storage engine that made memcached durable on disk
Multi-key transactions and a SQL query layer
Synchronous replication of every item across regions
mcq.why: Memcached stayed a simple get/set/delete server; Meta's work was the system built around it.

hook: Meta's web servers send cache reads over a protocol that loses some of them. Why is that a good deal?
title: UDP gets: drop 0.25% of reads, get 20% lower latency
body: Meta's web servers send memcache **gets over UDP** directly to cache servers, skipping TCP connection overhead. At peak about 0.25 percent of gets are dropped, and clients treat them as misses. In exchange, UDP gave about 20 percent lower latency than TCP via mcrouter. Only reads take this path. Sets and deletes, which must not vanish silently, still go over TCP. It works because a cache is allowed to lose data.
takeaway: When a lost message just looks like a miss, a lossy protocol is fine.
deeper:
**Why it's safe:** A dropped UDP get is indistinguishable from a miss. Correctness holds; the only cost is a little extra database load from those false misses.

**A subtle rule on errors:** After a UDP get error, Meta's clients skip the cache fill. They still get the value from the database but don't write it back, because an error may signal congestion and an extra set would add load.

**Why not UDP for writes:** A dropped delete is a lost invalidation, one of the three core consistency races, leaving stale data. A dropped set wastes a database read. So sets and deletes go over TCP through mcrouter, paying a little latency for reliable delivery.

**Why bother:** With many web servers talking to many cache servers, skipping per-connection state on the high-volume read path adds up.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes moving memcache deletes to UDP too, since gets work fine that way. What breaks?
quiz.a: A dropped get is just a miss, but a dropped delete is a lost invalidation: the cache keeps the old value while the database has the new one, possibly until the TTL expires.

mcq.q: About what share of Meta's UDP gets are dropped at peak?
options: About 0.25 percent
About 2.5 percent
About 10 percent
About 0.001 percent
mcq.why: Roughly 0.25 percent of gets drop at peak; clients treat them as misses, a small cost for about 20 percent lower latency.

predict.q: Meta sent memcache gets over UDP instead of TCP via mcrouter. What did it gain?
options: About 20% lower latency
About 2% lower latency
About 60% lower latency

hook: In 2014, a proxy in Meta's cache stack peaked near 5 billion requests per second. What was it doing?
title: mcrouter: a proxy layer near 5 billion requests/sec
body: At Meta, sets and deletes go over TCP through **mcrouter**, a proxy that runs on each web server. It speaks the memcached protocol, so applications talk to it as if it were memcached. It pools connections to cache servers and routes requests by key prefix, sending different key families to different pools. By 2014, mcrouter handled close to 5 billion requests per second at peak.
takeaway: Speak the app's protocol, and routing changes never touch app code.
deeper:
**Connection pooling:** Instead of every application thread opening connections to every cache server, mcrouter keeps shared connections, cutting connection counts and overhead.

**Routing by prefix:** A key's prefix decides its pool, so a low-value, high-churn key family can live in its own pool and not evict valuable keys.

**No special client:** Because it speaks the memcached protocol, applications need no new library. Routing policy, such as which pool a prefix maps to, changes without touching application code. Running on each web server keeps the proxy one local hop away.

**Invalidation relay:** McSqueal doesn't send deletes to every cache server directly. It sends batched deletes to a few mcrouter servers per cluster, which fan them out. That batching improved median deletes per packet 18 times.

quiz.q: You want to move one key family, say session:*, to its own server pool without redeploying 20 application services. How does Meta's mcrouter design make that easy?
quiz.a: mcrouter routes by key prefix and speaks the memcached protocol, so you change its routing config to map that prefix to a new pool; application code doesn't change.

mcq.q: How does mcrouter decide which pool a request goes to?
options: By the key's prefix
By the web server's region
By the value's size in bytes
By the key's hash slot number
mcq.why: Routing by key prefix lets different key families live in separate pools, isolating workloads.

hook: Hundreds of cache servers answer one web server instantly, all at once. Why is that a problem?
title: Incast: when too many answers arrive at once
body:
A Meta page load fetches hundreds of keys in parallel. Each cache server replies fast, so the replies converge on one web server at nearly the same instant. Switch buffers are finite. When they overflow, packets drop. That is **incast congestion**.

Meta's clients use flow control: a sliding window that caps outstanding requests. Responses arrive in manageable waves instead of one burst the switch can't buffer.
takeaway: Fan-out is a network problem, not just a latency problem.
deeper:
**Why fast servers make it worse:** Every cache server replies immediately, so their responses hit the same switch port together. The faster and more parallel the fan-out, the tighter the burst. Once the buffer is full, packets drop. Dropped packets mean retransmissions or, for UDP gets, false misses. Both hurt latency, and the page still waits for the slowest reply.

**Tuning the window:** Too small and the client serializes its requests, adding latency. Too large and incast returns. The right window keeps the network busy without flooding it.

**The general rule:** A page that fetches 500 keys waits for the slowest. Batch requests, cap fan-out, and watch for incast. Large values make it worse, since each response carries more bytes into the same buffers.

quiz.q: Page latency spikes whenever your service fetches many keys at once, yet each cache server reports low latency. Switch counters show drops. What's happening, and what's Meta's fix?
quiz.a: Incast: the parallel responses overflow the switch buffer at the client. Use flow control, a sliding window capping outstanding requests, so replies arrive in waves.

mcq.q: What causes incast congestion in a memcache cluster?
options: Many responses reaching one client at once and overflowing switch buffers
Many clients sending requests to one hot cache server
Deletes and sets sharing a single TCP connection
A cache server evicting keys faster than clients refill them
mcq.why: Parallel fan-out makes all replies converge on one client's switch port at once; finite buffers overflow and drop packets.

hook: Why would Meta deliberately split one cache fleet into separate groups of servers?
title: Pools: keep churny keys from evicting valuable ones
body: Caches evict when memory fills, and the survivors are whatever the eviction policy favors. A low-value, high-churn key set, written often and rarely reread, can push out the frequently read keys that were saving the database the most. Meta splits its memcached servers into **pools**: separate groups for workloads with different patterns.
