Eviction pressure in one pool can't touch another's hit ratio. mcrouter routes each key to its pool by prefix.
takeaway: Isolate workloads so one team's churn can't spend another team's memory.
deeper:
**Right treatment per workload:** Pools let each workload get what it needs. Keys with very high read rates can go into a replicated pool, with copies on several servers, which is how Meta spreads hot keys. Large, less popular items go into a shared regional pool instead of being duplicated in every frontend cluster.

**The failure it prevents:** Call it an eviction surprise. A new feature writes many low-value keys and evicts valuable ones. The fix is separate pools, as at Meta, or separate clusters per workload.

**The operational lesson:** Launching a new caching workload into a shared cache can silently raise database load for an unrelated service. Isolation also simplifies sizing, since each pool is sized by its own memory and throughput needs.

quiz.q: Two workloads share one memcached cluster: user profiles (read constantly) and a new activity log (written constantly, rarely read). What happens to profile hit ratio, and what's Meta's structural fix?
quiz.a: Activity-log writes fill memory and evict profile keys, dropping profile hit ratio and raising database load. Put each workload in its own pool, routed by key prefix.

mcq.q: What is the main purpose of Meta's separate memcached pools?
options: Stop one workload's churn from evicting another's valuable keys
Give each region its own copy of the primary database
Hold keys that failed servers can no longer serve
Store items too large for a single memcached server
mcq.why: Pools isolate workloads with different access patterns, so low-value, high-churn keys can't push out keys that spare the database.

hook: When a cache server dies, the obvious move is to spread its keys over the survivors. Meta refused. Why?
title: The Gutter pool: 1% idle servers cut failures by 99%
body: The obvious response to a dead cache server is rehashing its keys onto survivors. But load per key is uneven. A hot key landing on a healthy neighbor can overload it, and the failure cascades. So Meta keeps about 1 percent of memcached servers idle as a **Gutter pool**. When a server fails, clients send its traffic to Gutter instead. Gutter entries expire quickly, so stale data there is short-lived.
takeaway: Send a failed server's load to spare capacity, never onto a busy neighbor.
deeper:
**The chain Gutter breaks:** In a consistent-hashing cluster, a dead server's keys remap to neighbors. If it held a hot key, one neighbor suddenly gets that key's traffic on top of its own, may fail, and pushes the load onward. That is failure rehashing.

**What changes with Gutter:** The failed server's traffic goes to dedicated idle servers that have spare capacity by design. No healthy server's load changes. Misses in Gutter are filled from the database, and the short expiry keeps any stale entries brief.

**The price:** Roughly 1 in 100 servers sits mostly idle. The return is a 99 percent cut in client-visible failures. Along with warm restarts and cold cluster warmup, Gutter guards the first stage of the cache failure cascade: nodes failing and hit ratio dropping.

quiz.q: A cache node holding a celebrity's profile dies. Plan A rehashes its keys onto neighbors; plan B sends its traffic to a small idle pool. Which does Meta choose, and what goes wrong with the other?
quiz.a: Plan B, the Gutter pool. Under plan A the celebrity key lands on a busy neighbor, which can overload and die, pushing load onward in a cascade.

mcq.q: Why do Meta's Gutter pool entries expire quickly?
options: To keep any stale data in Gutter short-lived
Because Gutter servers have very little memory
So Gutter can hand keys back through rehashing
Because Gutter entries are replicated across regions
mcq.why: Gutter serves a failed server's traffic temporarily; short expiry limits how long any stale value there can be served.

hook: Meta copies popular data into every frontend cluster but keeps big, rarely read items in one place. Why?
title: Duplicate the popular, share the rare: Meta's regions
body: Inside a Meta region, several frontend clusters share one storage cluster. Each frontend cluster has its own full cache, so popular data is duplicated: clusters stay self-contained and extra copies spread load. Less popular, large items go into a shared **regional pool**, because copying them everywhere wastes memory for little hit-ratio gain. Across regions, one region holds the primary databases and others hold replicas, and invalidations flow with MySQL replication.
takeaway: Duplicate what earns its memory; share what doesn't.
deeper:
**Why duplicate:** Duplicating popular data costs memory but keeps each frontend cluster self-contained. Web servers read from nearby cache servers, a failure in one cluster doesn't affect the others, and popular keys get spread across more copies.

**Why share:** For large, rarely read items the trade flips. One shared regional pool serves every frontend cluster in the region.

**Keeping every copy honest:** McSqueal on each database extracts keys from committed SQL and broadcasts deletes to all frontend clusters in the region, batched through mcrouter. Across regions, invalidations travel with MySQL replication, so a replica region's caches are cleaned in step with its data.

**The cross-region gap:** Remote markers cover read-after-write. A writer in a non-primary region sets a marker, writes to the primary database, and deletes the local key; readers seeing the marker go to the primary region.

quiz.q: You run four frontend clusters in a region. A large, rarely viewed report object keeps getting evicted from each cluster's cache. What would Meta's design do with it?
quiz.a: Put it in a shared regional pool used by all four clusters instead of duplicating it in each cluster's cache, saving memory for little loss in hit ratio.

mcq.q: Where does Meta put large, less popular cache items?
options: In a shared regional pool used by all frontend clusters
In every frontend cluster's own full cache
In the Gutter pool until they are requested again
In the storage cluster's MySQL buffer pool
mcq.why: Duplicating rare, large items in every cluster wastes memory; one shared pool per region holds them while popular data stays duplicated.

hook: A brand-new cache cluster comes online completely empty. How do you fill it without flooding the database?
title: Cold Cluster Warmup: full capacity in hours, not days
body: An empty cache sends every read to the database, and a new Meta frontend cluster starts exactly that way. **Cold Cluster Warmup** lets the cold cluster read its misses from a warm cluster's cache instead, bringing it to full capacity in a few hours instead of a few days. To avoid races during warmup, deletes to the cold cluster carry a two-second hold-off.
takeaway: Fill a cold cache from a warm peer, not from the database.
deeper:
**Why cold is dangerous:** A cache at 99 percent hit ratio sends 1 percent of reads to the database; an empty cache sends 100 percent. A new cluster serving real traffic would multiply database load until it filled.

**Why a peer works:** Each frontend cluster holds its own full cache of similar content, so a warm neighbor already has most of what the cold one needs. The database is spared.

**The race the hold-off closes:** The cold cluster fetches a value from the warm cluster just as a write deletes that key in both. If the fetched copy predates the delete, the cold cluster could set stale data right after its own delete. The two-second hold-off blocks sets for a key briefly after it is deleted in the cold cluster.

**Where it fits:** Warmup from a warm peer sits alongside slow rolling restarts, warm restarts and cross-region replication as a cure for cold caches.

quiz.q: During warmup, a cold cluster fetches a key from a warm peer while a write deletes that key in both clusters. Without protection, what can go wrong, and what did Meta add?
quiz.a: The cold cluster can set the pre-delete value after its own delete, caching stale data. Meta's deletes to the cold cluster carry a two-second hold-off that blocks such late sets.

mcq.q: Where does a cold Meta cluster read its misses during Cold Cluster Warmup?
options: From a warm cluster's cache
From the regional primary database
From the Gutter pool
From a replica region's cache
mcq.why: Reading misses from a warm peer's cache spares the database and fills the new cluster in hours instead of days.

predict.q: Meta's Cold Cluster Warmup fills a new cluster from a warm peer. How long does reaching full capacity take?
options: A few hours instead of a few days
A few minutes instead of an hour
A few days instead of a few weeks

hook: Meta patched memcache races one by one. Then TAO avoided many of them by design. How?
title: TAO: a graph-aware cache that funnels writes via leaders
body: In Meta's memcache design, many independent web servers read the database, fill the cache and send deletes, and races come from their uncoordinated interleaving. **TAO** took over many social-graph reads with a different shape. It understands the graph model. Follower tiers serve clients. Leader tiers, one per shard, read and write MySQL and send invalidations to followers. All writes to a shard go through one leader, so many look-aside races vanish by design.
takeaway: Give each shard one writer, and ordering races have nowhere to happen.
deeper:
**One ordered stream:** The leader for a shard is the single path for writes to that shard's data. It writes MySQL, then invalidates the follower tiers. Instead of many competing clients, there is one ordered stream of changes per shard, which removes much of the ambiguity about which update came last. TAO handled a billion reads per second in 2013.

**Patching versus redesigning:** The memcache layer needed leases for stale sets, McSqueal for lost deletes, and remote markers for replica lag. TAO attacks a common cause, uncoordinated writers, rather than each symptom.

**Knowing the data:** TAO caches graph objects and associations rather than opaque keys, a fit for Meta's graph-heavy workload.

**A familiar pattern:** It resembles the integrated-cache idea behind Uber's CacheFront: when the data platform owns the cache, application code cannot forget to invalidate.

quiz.q: Why would funneling every write for a shard through one leader tier remove the 'two writers update the cache in opposite order' problem?
quiz.a: With a single leader writing MySQL and then invalidating followers, there's one ordered stream of changes per shard, so no competing writers exist whose updates could arrive out of order.

mcq.q: How does TAO avoid many look-aside races?
options: All writes to a shard go through one leader tier
Every cached value carries a 64-bit lease token
Followers refuse to cache any recently written key
Clients send deletes over TCP instead of UDP
mcq.why: Serializing a shard's writes through one leader, which then invalidates followers, gives a single ordered write path.

hook: By 2017, several Meta caching teams were each building the same features. What did Meta do about it?
title: CacheLib: one caching engine instead of many rebuilt ones
body: By 2017 Meta had many separate caching systems, for the CDN, the social graph, storage and application caches. Each team was rebuilding the same features. **CacheLib** is a C++ caching library that extracts the common core. First deployed in 2017, it powered over 70 services by 2020. Its big ideas: hybrid DRAM plus flash, two flash engines, flash admission policies and warm restarts.

stat.label: Meta services powered by CacheLib by 2020

takeaway: When every team rebuilds the same engine, make the engine a library.
deeper:
**Engineering economics:** Features built by one team did not help another, and the same work was done several times over. A shared library turns that duplicated effort into one investment: an improvement in CacheLib reaches every service that links it.

**Why a library, not a server:** A library can slot into very different systems, from CDN edge caches to social-graph and storage caches. Each service keeps its own protocol and deployment while sharing the caching engine.

**What the paper measured:** One caching server can replace tens of backend database servers, thanks to about 20 times higher throughput and hit ratios above 80 percent. And real workloads had popularity less skewed and more volatile than textbook models, which strengthens the case for larger caches and therefore for flash. The CDN, whose caches serve 70 percent of Meta's web requests, was one of the systems CacheLib unified.

quiz.q: Four teams at your company each maintain their own cache server, and each has separately built the same eviction and monitoring features. What did Meta do in this situation, and why a library rather than one shared server?
quiz.a: It extracted the common core into CacheLib, a C++ library. A library can embed in very different systems, each keeping its own protocol and deployment while sharing one engine.

mcq.q: What problem was CacheLib built to solve?
options: Separate caching teams rebuilding the same features
Memcached's lack of multi-key transactions
Cross-region replication lag for social-graph caches
Lost invalidations when application servers crashed
mcq.why: Meta's CDN, graph, storage and application caches each rebuilt the same core; CacheLib extracted it into one shared library.

hook: DRAM is fast but pricey. A database trip is slow. What can sit in between, and what does it cost you?
title: DRAM first, then flash: many times more cache per dollar
body: Many workloads have a long tail: a huge set of items, each read occasionally. Keeping them all in DRAM is too expensive. Letting them miss sends a steady stream of reads to the backend. CacheLib adds a middle tier. It looks in DRAM first, then **flash**. Flash gives many times more capacity per dollar than DRAM and still serves sub-millisecond reads. Same budget, a much bigger cache.
takeaway: Hot items earn DRAM. The long tail earns flash, not a database trip.
deeper:
**The lookup path:**
1. Check DRAM.
2. On a DRAM miss, check flash.
3. Only then go to the backend.

**Problem one, endurance:** Flash wears out with writes, and cache contents churn fast. Writing every item evicted from DRAM would burn through devices. Admission policies control the write rate.

**Problem two, indexing:** A DRAM index entry for every item on a large flash device can cost too much DRAM, especially for small items. CacheLib's Small Object Cache avoids a per-item index.

**When it pays:** When the working set is 10 times bigger than affordable DRAM, a DRAM-only cache has a poor hit ratio and the backend pays. DRAM plus flash can hold the long tail, at the price of slightly slower flash hits.

quiz.q: Your cache's hit ratio plateaus because the working set is far bigger than the DRAM you can afford. More DRAM servers are too expensive. What does CacheLib's design suggest, and what new problem must you manage?
quiz.a: Add a flash tier behind DRAM: many times more capacity per dollar with sub-millisecond reads. You must manage flash wear, limiting writes with admission policies.

mcq.q: In CacheLib's hybrid cache, what happens on a DRAM miss?
options: It checks flash before going to the backend
It goes straight to the backend database
It asks a peer server's DRAM for the item
It returns a miss and fills flash later
mcq.why: CacheLib looks in DRAM first, then flash, and only falls back to the backend if both miss.

hook: Index every tiny object on flash in DRAM, and you spend the DRAM flash was meant to save. The fix?
title: Two flash engines: index big items, hash tiny ones
body: Indexing cost grows with the number of items, not their size. So CacheLib runs two flash engines. The **Large Object Cache** (LOC) holds items of 2 KB and up, aligned to 4 KB flash pages, with a compact DRAM index. The **Small Object Cache** (SOC) holds items under 2 KB by hashing them into 4 KB buckets on flash, so it needs almost no DRAM index. Small objects, like graph edges and nodes, are very common.
takeaway: For tiny items, compute the location; don't store it.
deeper:
**Why LOC can index:** For large items, one index entry per item is tiny next to the data, so LOC keeps a DRAM index and places each item directly on page-aligned flash.

**Why SOC can't:** A flash device holds an enormous number of sub-2 KB objects. A DRAM entry for each could approach the size of the objects themselves, defeating the point of using flash to save DRAM. Instead, an item's key hashes to one 4 KB bucket. Reading it means reading that bucket and searching inside.

**Wear, too:** Flash layouts designed to limit application-level write amplification are one of two ways CacheLib reduces flash wear, alongside admission policies. Writing in 4 KB pages and buckets fits how the device works.

quiz.q: A cache stores tens of billions of social-graph edges, each well under 2 KB, on flash. Why would a per-item DRAM index be a bad idea, and what does CacheLib do instead?
quiz.a: The index would need an entry per edge, costing DRAM comparable to the data itself. CacheLib's Small Object Cache hashes each item into a 4 KB flash bucket, so its location is computed.

mcq.q: What item size separates CacheLib's Large and Small Object Caches?
options: 2 KB
4 KB
512 bytes
64 KB
mcq.why: Items of 2 KB and larger go to LOC with a DRAM index; items under 2 KB are hashed into 4 KB buckets by SOC.

hook: Your flash cache is wearing out, and the culprit is its own eviction traffic. What's the simplest fix?
title: Flash admission: don't write every evicted item
body: Flash wears out with writes, and cache contents churn fast. Write every item evicted from DRAM to flash and the devices die young. So CacheLib uses **admission policies**: it does not write every evicted item to flash. The default admits items with a fixed probability. That gives direct control over the flash write rate, and so over device life, at the cost of leaving some items off flash.
takeaway: Flash endurance is a budget. Admission policy is how you spend it.
deeper:
**The core trade-off:** Admit everything and you maximize flash hits but burn endurance. Admit too little and flash sits underused while the backend pays for misses.

**Why a fixed probability:** It is simple and predictable. The write rate scales directly with the admission probability, so you can set it to match the device's endurance budget.

**Two ways CacheLib limits wear:** Admission policies that write only some evicted items to flash. And flash layouts, LOC and SOC, designed to limit application-level write amplification.

**The price, stated plainly:** Flash endurance must be managed by controlling the write rate, and flash hits are slightly slower than DRAM hits. Aerospike's hybrid layout faces a related trade-off as a database rather than a cache, where the flash holds data of record.

quiz.q: Your flash cache writes twice what the drives' endurance budget allows. With CacheLib's default admission policy, what single knob do you turn, and what do you give up?
quiz.a: Lower the fixed admission probability; write rate scales with it. You give up some flash hits, since fewer evicted items are admitted, so more misses reach the backend.

mcq.q: What does CacheLib's default flash admission policy do?
options: Admits evicted items with a fixed probability
Admits only items read at least twice
Admits every item evicted from DRAM
Admits items only during off-peak hours
mcq.why: A fixed admission probability directly sets the flash write rate, which controls device wear.

hook: Every code deploy restarts your cache, and every restart empties it. What if it didn't have to?
title: Warm restarts: a deploy shouldn't empty the cache
body: Production caches restart often for code deploys. Many of Meta's run less than 7 days between restarts. A normal restart leaves the cache empty, and it refills from the backend, pounding the database. CacheLib supports **warm restarts**: it saves its state before shutting down and reattaches after the restart, so the cache comes back full. Frequent deploys stop meaning frequent cold caches.
takeaway: If you deploy weekly, a cold restart is a weekly load test on your database.
deeper:
**It compounds with scale:** If each server restarts every few days, some fraction of the fleet is always cold and refilling. Restart many at once, as in a fleet-wide deploy, and the database sees a surge.

**The mitigation menu:** Roll restarts slowly, restart warm (CacheLib), warm new clusters from a peer (Meta), or replicate across regions (EVCache, CacheFront).

**Why warm restarts are cheapest:** The data never leaves the machine. Instead of rebuilding from the database or copying from another cluster, the new process reattaches to the saved state.

**Big caches need it most:** A DRAM plus flash cache holding the long tail fills slowly, because long-tail items are by definition rarely requested. Losing that on every deploy would erase much of the benefit of having a big cache at all.

quiz.q: Your team deploys cache servers every few days, in batches of 20 percent of the fleet. After each batch, database load spikes. Name two fixes and say which is cheapest.
quiz.a: Warm restarts (save and reattach state), slower rolling restarts, or warming from a peer. Warm restarts are cheapest: the data never leaves the machine.

mcq.q: How does a CacheLib warm restart avoid an empty cache?
options: It saves its state before shutdown and reattaches after restart
It copies every item from a peer cluster during startup
It replays the database commit log to rebuild entries
It serves from a replica until the new process fills
mcq.why: The process saves cache state and the new version reattaches to it, so the cache comes back full without backend reads.

predict.q: Meta's CacheLib paper looked at how long production caches run between restarts. What's common?
options: Less than 7 days
About 6 months
About a year

hook: Textbooks say a few items get almost all the traffic. Meta measured real caches. Were the textbooks right?
title: Real workloads are flatter than Zipf, so bigger caches pay
body: Textbook caching assumes Zipf popularity: a few items take most of the traffic, so a small cache catches most requests. The CacheLib paper measured production and found popularity often less skewed. Meta's social-graph and CDN workloads had a **Zipf alpha** around 0.55, spreading traffic across more items. Popularity also shifted within hours. Both make caching harder and larger caches more valuable. That is the case for flash.

stat.label: Zipf skew of Meta's social-graph and CDN traffic

takeaway: The flatter the popularity curve, the more cache you need to buy.
deeper:
**What alpha means:** The steeper the skew, the more a small cache of top items captures. With a flatter distribution like alpha around 0.55, hit ratio grows slowly with cache size: to catch most requests you must hold a much larger share of all items.

**Churn adds pressure:** Yesterday's hot items cool off and new ones appear within hours. The cache constantly replaces its contents, which also raises write pressure on flash.

**Why flash follows:** Bigger caches are affordable only on cheaper media. DRAM plus flash can hold the long tail that a DRAM-only cache cannot.

**Why each point matters:** In an illustrative example with 2 million reads per second at peak, every 1 percent of hit ratio gained removes 20,000 database reads per second.

quiz.q: You sized a DRAM cache assuming steep Zipf popularity, expecting a small cache to catch most reads. Production hit ratio disappoints. What did Meta's measurements suggest is going on, and what's the lever?
quiz.a: Popularity is flatter than textbook Zipf (alpha around 0.55) and shifts within hours, so a small cache misses a lot. Grow capacity cheaply with a flash tier.

mcq.q: What did the CacheLib paper find about real popularity distributions?
options: Less skewed than textbook Zipf, and changing within hours
More skewed than Zipf, so tiny caches suffice
Exactly Zipf, but stable over weeks
Uniform, so caching gives almost no benefit
mcq.why: Social-graph and CDN traffic had Zipf alpha around 0.55 and fast-shifting popularity, making larger caches more valuable.

hook: How can a database promise that every single lookup costs at most one flash read?
title: Aerospike: index in DRAM, records on SSD, one flash read
body: A B-tree on SSD can need a chain of index page reads before it reaches a record. Aerospike avoids that. Its **Hybrid Memory Architecture** keeps the primary index in DRAM and the records on SSD. Finding a record never touches flash; fetching it takes one read. So every lookup costs at most one flash read. Unlike CacheLib, this is a database, not a cache: the records on SSD are the real data.
takeaway: Keep the map in memory, and the territory costs one trip.
deeper:
**A cousin of CacheLib's LOC:** Both keep a compact index in DRAM and the bulk of data on flash, so a lookup goes straight to the right location. The difference is role. CacheLib can lose data and refill from a backend. Aerospike's SSD holds the data of record.

**Predictable latency:** The worst case is a single flash read, which makes tail latency easier to reason about.

**The trade-off:** DRAM cost for the index scales with the number of records. That is exactly the problem CacheLib's Small Object Cache sidesteps for tiny items by hashing into buckets.

**The shared economics:** Flash caching and Aerospike-style layouts both extend capacity cheaply, provided flash writes are controlled. The same hardware facts shape caches and primary stores alike.

quiz.q: A key-value store keeps its index on SSD alongside the data, and lookups sometimes take several flash reads. What would switching to Aerospike's layout change, and what would it cost?
quiz.a: With the index in DRAM, every lookup takes at most one flash read, for the record itself. The cost is DRAM for the index, which grows with the record count.

mcq.q: How does Aerospike's Hybrid Memory Architecture guarantee at most one flash read per lookup?
options: The primary index lives in DRAM; only the record read touches SSD
Records are hashed into 4 KB buckets that are read whole
Every record is cached in DRAM after its first read
The index and record share one flash page
mcq.why: Locating a record uses the in-memory index, so the only flash access is reading the record itself.

hook: The working set is 10× the DRAM you can afford. A DRAM-only cache is losing. What changes the math?
title: Flash caches change the cost curve of caching
body: When the working set is 10 times bigger than affordable DRAM, a DRAM-only cache has a poor hit ratio, and the backend pays for every miss. A DRAM plus flash cache can hold the **long tail** instead. The costs are real but manageable: flash endurance, controlled by admission policies that limit write rate, and slightly higher latency for flash hits than DRAM hits.
takeaway: Size the cache to the working set, then pick media that make it affordable.
deeper:
**The first question:** How big is the working set compared with the DRAM you can afford? If the hot set fits comfortably in DRAM, flash adds complexity for little gain. If it is much larger, DRAM-only caching leaves a hit-ratio gap that shows up as database load. CacheLib's flatter-than-Zipf measurements make that gap costlier.

**The leverage:** Database load equals read rate times one minus hit ratio, so small hit-ratio gains remove large amounts of database work. In an illustrative example, each 1 percent gained removes 20,000 database reads per second at peak, and a full 1 billion-profile set of about 1.1 TB might fit on a few flash-backed servers.

**Designing for the costs:** Pick an admission probability that matches device endurance, and accept that a flash hit is slower than DRAM but still far faster than a database read.

quiz.q: A reviewer proposes adding a flash tier to a cache whose entire hot set already fits in DRAM with room to spare. Is it worth it?
quiz.a: Probably not. Flash pays off when the working set far exceeds affordable DRAM; here it would add complexity, flash wear and slower hits for little hit-ratio gain.

mcq.q: What are the two main costs of adding flash to a DRAM cache?
options: Flash wear and slightly slower flash hits
Data loss and higher write latency
Stale reads and more invalidation traffic
Higher DRAM use and more hot keys
mcq.why: Flash endurance limits write rate (managed by admission policies), and flash hits are a bit slower than DRAM hits.

hook: Netflix stores every cached item several times over, once per availability zone. What does that memory buy?
title: EVCache: memcached with a full copy in every zone
body: **EVCache** (Ephemeral Volatile Cache) is Netflix's distributed cache built on memcached and designed for AWS. Clients spread keys with consistent hashing (Ketama). A typical setup keeps a full copy of the data in each availability zone. Reads go to the local zone. Writes go to all zones. If an item is missing locally, from instance failure or eviction, the client reads it from another zone.
takeaway: One copy per zone turns a lost node into a cross-zone read, not a miss.
deeper:
**Three problems, one layout:** Reads stay inside the zone, so latency is low and cross-zone hops are rare. Losing an instance doesn't mean a cold cache, since other zones still hold the data. And every zone has a copy of a popular key, so hot-key reads spread naturally.

**The cost:** Every item is stored once per zone, and every write or delete must reach every zone. In an illustrative sizing, one copy per zone across three zones turns about 220 GB into about 660 GB.

**Smart client, plain servers:** The client handles hashing, zone selection, writes to all zones and fallback reads, so the servers stay plain memcached. That same client is where Netflix hooks in cross-region replication, keeping other regions' caches warm.

quiz.q: An EVCache instance in one zone fails and loses its items. A user in that zone requests one of them. What happens, and why doesn't the database take the hit?
quiz.a: The client misses locally and reads the item from another zone's copy. Because each zone holds a full copy, the lost instance becomes a cross-zone read, not a database query.

mcq.q: In a typical EVCache setup, where do reads and writes go?
options: Reads to the local zone; writes to all zones
Reads to all zones; writes to the local zone
Reads and writes to one primary zone
Reads to any zone; writes to a Kafka queue
mcq.why: Each zone holds a full copy, so reads stay local while writes must update every zone's copy.

hook: Netflix replicates its cache across regions, yet never puts the cached value in the queue. Why?
title: EVCache's cross-region pipeline ships keys, not values
body: If a failover region's caches were cold, the sudden traffic would crush its databases. So EVCache replicates across regions. The app writes to its local EVCache. The client publishes a small **metadata event**, the key but not the value, to Kafka. A replication reader consumes it, reads the latest value from local EVCache, and sends it to a replication writer in the other region, which writes it there.
takeaway: Queue the key, fetch the value late: smaller messages, fresher data.
deeper:
**Smaller pipeline:** Keys are tiny compared with values, so Kafka carries far less data. Both sets and deletes enter the pipeline, so the remote cache tracks the local one.

**Fresher data:** Because the reader fetches the value from local EVCache when it processes the event, it replicates the newest value, not whatever was current when the event was published. A key written several times in quick succession still ships its latest state.

**The scale (2024):** About 200 memcached clusters, 22,000 server instances, 400 million operations per second, 30 million replication events globally, and about 2 trillion items totaling 14.3 PB.

**Not unique to Netflix:** Uber's CacheFront also replicates Redis writes so the remote region has a warm cache for failover.

quiz.q: A key is updated three times within a second, so EVCache publishes three events. What value lands in the remote region, and why is that better than shipping values through Kafka?
quiz.a: The latest value, since the reader fetches from local EVCache when it processes each event. Shipping values would enlarge every message and could replicate outdated ones.

mcq.q: What does EVCache publish to Kafka for cross-region replication?
options: A small metadata event with the key, not the value
The full value with a version timestamp
A batch of every changed value each minute
A copy of the database binlog entry
mcq.why: Only the key goes through Kafka; the reader fetches the latest value from local EVCache, keeping messages small and data fresh.

hook: Netflix evacuates a failing region. The healthy region's databases are fine. What could still sink them?
title: Netflix: a warm cache is part of disaster recovery
body: When a region fails, Netflix moves all its traffic to other regions. The survivors' databases are sized for their own normal miss traffic. If the evacuated users' data isn't in the local cache, every one of their reads misses. A cold cache during failover would turn a regional outage into a global database overload. So Netflix keeps failover caches warm on purpose, through **cross-region replication**.
takeaway: A failover plan with a cold cache is a plan to overload the next region.
deeper:
**The load-bearing cache, taken to its end:** A region's databases handle only what misses its cache. During failover, the surviving region also serves users from the failed one. If their data is cold, the combined miss rate can far exceed what the databases can take, and the outage spreads.

**The price of warmth:** Continuous replication traffic and memory in every region, whether or not a failover ever happens. Netflix pays it because failover has to work when it's needed.

**Not just Netflix:** Uber's CacheFront replicates Redis writes across regions for the same reason.

**The full menu for cold caches:** Slow rolling restarts, CacheLib warm restarts, Meta's cold cluster warmup, and cross-region replication, each sized for a different scale of event, from one node to a whole region.

quiz.q: Your DR plan fails traffic over to a second region whose cache holds only that region's users. Its databases run near capacity at peak. Why might failover fail, and what's the fix?
quiz.a: The evacuated users' reads all miss the cold cache and land on those databases, pushing them past capacity. Replicate cache writes across regions so the failover cache is warm.

mcq.q: Why does Netflix keep caches in its failover regions warm?
options: A cold cache during failover would overload the surviving region's databases
Warm caches let Netflix skip replicating its databases across regions
Kafka can only replicate data into caches that are already warm
Cold caches return stale data after a failover
mcq.why: Redirected users' reads would all miss a cold cache, sending a surge to the surviving databases and spreading the outage.

hook: The cache has the RAM, but new items keep getting evicted anyway. Where is the memory stuck?
title: Twemcache: Twitter's operational fork of memcached
body: Twitter forked memcached 1.4.4 into **Twemcache**, and the main changes were operational. One problem it tackled was **slab calcification**. Memcached allocates memory in size classes. If item sizes shift, memory stays stuck in classes that no longer match the workload, so the cache is effectively smaller than its RAM. Twemcache added pluggable eviction, including item LRU, random eviction and slab-level eviction, plus lock-free stats and a lockless command logger. Pelikan replaced it in 2021.
takeaway: Memory stuck in the wrong size class is memory you pay for but can't use.
deeper:
**How calcification happens:** Memcached carves memory into slabs divided into fixed size classes, and each item goes into the class that fits it. When the workload's item sizes drift, memory already assigned to the old classes stays there even though new items need a different class. Hit ratio suffers. Slab-level eviction frees whole slabs so memory can move to the classes that need it now.

**Observability without contention:** Lock-free statistics let operators watch the cache without adding contention on hot paths. A lockless command logger captures what a server is receiving, for debugging in production without slowing it down.

**The lineage:** Twitter's lesson was that at scale, memory efficiency and operational behavior matter as much as raw speed. Pelikan and its Segcache engine continued that work after Twemcache retired in 2021.

quiz.q: A cache's workload shifts from mostly small items to mostly large ones. Hit ratio drops though total memory hasn't changed. What's the likely cause in a memcached-style allocator, and what did Twemcache add?
quiz.a: Slab calcification: memory is stuck in size classes for small items. Twemcache added slab-level eviction to free whole slabs and reassign that memory.

mcq.q: What is slab calcification?
options: Memory stuck in size classes that no longer match the workload
Expired items lingering because no one reads them
Hot keys pinned to a single slab on one server
Slabs fragmenting after many small writes to flash
mcq.why: Memory assigned to old size classes stays there when item sizes shift, so the cache effectively shrinks.

hook: Expired items can sit in cache memory long after they die. How did Twitter's Segcache stop paying for them?
title: Segcache: expire whole segments, not single items
body: **Pelikan** is Twitter's framework for building cache servers from shared parts, now written in Rust. It separates control and data planes at runtime and uses lockless data structures so worker threads never block. Its **Segcache** engine (NSDI 2021) groups objects with similar expiry times into segments, so expired data is removed in bulk. It used 22 to 60 percent less memory than state-of-the-art designs on tested workloads and reached close to 8× memcached's throughput at 24 threads.
takeaway: Group items by when they die, and cleanup becomes one cheap sweep.
deeper:
**Why grouping by expiry helps:** When items with different TTLs are mixed, expired ones linger until something happens to look at them, and removing them one at a time is costly. Segcache places objects with similar expiry times in the same segment. When the segment's time comes, the whole thing goes at once.

**The numbers, carefully:** 22 to 60 percent less memory than state-of-the-art designs, on the tested workloads, with small objects as the engine's focus. Close to 8 times memcached's throughput at 24 threads.

**Why threads scale:** Pelikan's goal is that worker threads never block, so it uses lockless data structures and keeps control-plane work off the data path.

**A familiar motive:** Like CacheLib at Meta, Pelikan builds cache servers from shared, reusable parts instead of starting from scratch. It replaced Twemcache at Twitter in 2021.

quiz.q: A cache holds billions of small items with TTLs from seconds to days, all mixed together. Why does per-item expiry waste memory, and how does Segcache change it?
quiz.a: Expired items linger until something touches them, and removing them one by one is costly. Segcache groups items with similar expiry into segments and drops whole segments at once.

mcq.q: How does Segcache organize objects?
options: Into segments of objects with similar expiry times
Into slabs by object size class
Into 4 KB flash buckets by key hash
Into per-thread arenas by write order
mcq.why: Grouping by expiry time lets expired data be removed in bulk, a whole segment at once.

predict.q: Segcache was benchmarked against memcached at 24 threads. What throughput did it reach?
options: Close to 8× memcached
About 1.5× memcached
About the same as memcached

hook: 50 bytes of bookkeeping per item sounds like nothing. At what point does it cost terabytes of RAM?
title: 50 bytes per item becomes terabytes at trillions
body: Twitter's lesson: at scale, a cache's memory efficiency and TTL handling matter as much as raw speed. **Per-object overhead** of 50 bytes is nothing for one item. Across a trillion items it is 50 TB of RAM spent on bookkeeping, holding no data at all. Engines that shave metadata and reclaim expired items promptly let the same hardware hold far more of the working set.

stat.label: of RAM for 50 bytes × 1 trillion items

takeaway: At a trillion items, every byte of overhead is a terabyte.
deeper:
**Memory efficiency is hit ratio:** With the same DRAM, a leaner engine holds more items. More items means a higher hit ratio, which means less database load. In an illustrative example with 2 million reads per second at peak, each 1 percent of hit ratio is 20,000 database reads per second.

**The scale is real:** Netflix's EVCache held about 2 trillion items totaling 14.3 PB in 2024.

**TTL handling, same logic:** Expired items sitting in memory until evicted are dead weight. An engine like Segcache that removes them in bulk frees memory for live data.

**Small objects hurt most:** Overhead is proportionally worst on tiny items, which is why Segcache and CacheLib's Small Object Cache both focus on them. Even a sizing example with 1 KB profiles assumes about 100 bytes of cache overhead each, roughly 10 percent.

quiz.q: A new cache engine cuts per-item metadata from 50 to 30 bytes. Your fleet holds 2 trillion items. How much RAM does that free, and why might it matter more than a throughput gain?
quiz.a: About 40 TB (20 bytes × 2 trillion). That memory holds more items, raising hit ratio and cutting database load, which a faster engine alone doesn't do.

mcq.q: Why can shrinking per-item metadata raise a large cache's hit ratio?
options: The same RAM then holds more items
Smaller metadata makes each lookup faster
Less metadata means fewer invalidations
Smaller items expire sooner and free space
mcq.why: Memory saved on bookkeeping holds more data, so more of the working set fits and fewer reads miss.

section: 6.10 Uber CacheFront: a cache inside the database
hook: What if application teams never wrote a single line of cache code, and still got a cache?
title: Uber CacheFront: the query engine owns the cache
body: Instead of every team building look-aside logic, Uber put the cache inside Docstore's query engine. This is **CacheFront** (2024). On reads, the engine checks Redis first, returns cached rows, fetches the rest from the storage engine, and fills Redis asynchronously. For invalidation, Flux tails the MySQL binlog and invalidates or updates Redis within seconds, while the write path also invalidates directly. Applications just query Docstore.
takeaway: When the platform owns the cache, no team can forget the delete.
deeper:
**Read-through, in practice:** The cache layer, not the application, fills on a miss. Placing it in the query engine gives every Docstore user the same tested behavior.

**Partial hits:** A query for several rows returns the cached ones and fetches only the missing rows from storage. Filling Redis asynchronously keeps the fill off the request's critical path.

**Two invalidation channels:** The write path's direct invalidation gives fast freshness in the normal case. Flux, tailing the binlog, is the reliable backstop: because the binlog is durable and ordered, a crashed write path cannot lose an invalidation. It mirrors Meta's McSqueal.

**Layered on top:** Timestamp checks against stale fills, negative caching for missing rows, Redis sharded independently of the database, and cross-region replication for failover.

quiz.q: CacheFront's write path already invalidates Redis directly. Why also run Flux on the binlog, and why keep the direct path if Flux exists?
quiz.a: Direct invalidation gives fast freshness; Flux is durable and ordered, so invalidations survive a crashed write path. Flux takes up to seconds, so the direct path serves fresh reads sooner.

mcq.q: Where does Uber's CacheFront live?
options: Inside Docstore's query engine
In each application's client library
In a proxy on every web server
Inside the MySQL storage engine
mcq.why: Putting the cache in the query engine means applications just query Docstore and get caching without writing cache logic.

section: 6.10 Uber CacheFront: a cache inside the database
hook: A lookup for a row that doesn't exist misses every time. Can a cache even help with that?
title: Cache the misses too: negative caching and timestamp guards
body: Without help, a lookup for a missing row always misses, because there's nothing to cache, and always hits MySQL. CacheFront uses **negative caching**: rows that don't exist are cached with a flag, so repeated lookups for absent keys are served from Redis. It also blocks stale fills. Lua scripts in Redis compare row timestamps, so older data can never overwrite newer data, even from a delayed asynchronous fill.
takeaway: 'Not found' is an answer too. Cache it.
deeper:
**The hidden load source:** If many requests look up missing rows repeatedly, from a client bug or a common probe pattern, the database takes that load in full no matter how high the hit ratio is for existing rows. Caching the absence turns those lookups into hits.

**Its own staleness:** A cached 'missing' flag can go stale too. If the row is later created, the negative entry is wrong until it is invalidated or expires, like any other cached value.

**Timestamps instead of tokens:** This is Uber's answer to the stale-set race that Meta solved with leases. Each cached row carries its timestamp, and a Lua script, running atomically inside Redis, writes the incoming row only if it is newer than what's already there. A delayed fill or a lagging source can't resurrect old data.

quiz.q: A buggy client repeatedly looks up user IDs that were never created. Your hit ratio for real users is 99 percent, yet the database is busy. Why, and what does CacheFront do about it?
quiz.a: Missing rows never get cached, so every lookup falls through to the database. CacheFront caches non-existent rows with a flag, so repeat lookups hit Redis.

mcq.q: How does CacheFront prevent a delayed fill from overwriting fresher data?
options: Lua scripts in Redis compare row timestamps before writing
Each miss receives a 64-bit lease token from Redis
Fills are rejected for two seconds after any delete
Flux holds back fills until the binlog catches up
mcq.why: The atomic script writes the incoming row only if its timestamp is newer than the cached one.

section: 6.10 Uber CacheFront: a cache inside the database
hook: Uber could have mapped each Redis cluster to one database shard. It deliberately didn't. Why not?
title: Shard the cache apart from the database
body: Suppose each Redis cluster mirrored one database shard. When a Redis cluster fails, its whole miss load lands on that single shard, sized only for normal miss traffic. CacheFront instead shards Redis by **partition key**, independently of database sharding. A failed cluster holds keys from many shards, so its misses spread thinly across all of them. CacheFront also replicates Redis writes to a remote region, so failover finds a warm cache.
takeaway: Align cache shards with database shards, and one cache failure picks one victim.
deeper:
**Blast radius:** With one-to-one mapping, a Redis failure concentrates all its misses on one database shard, which may not survive. With independent sharding, each Redis cluster holds keys from many database shards, so a failure adds a modest increase to each. No single shard takes the hit.

**Answering the senior question:** If this cache were empty, could the database survive? For a single cluster failure, spreading misses makes the answer yes far more often.

**The bigger failure:** Losing a whole region. Like Netflix EVCache, CacheFront replicates cache writes so the failover region's Redis already holds what the failed region's users will request.

**The shared lesson:** Warm caches are part of disaster recovery, and cache topology is part of database capacity planning.

quiz.q: Your Redis clusters map one-to-one to database shards. One Redis cluster crashes. What happens, and how would CacheFront's design change the outcome?
quiz.a: Its entire miss load hits one database shard, which may overload. Sharding Redis independently spreads a failed cluster's misses across all database shards, so each sees only a small increase.

mcq.q: Why does CacheFront shard Redis independently of database sharding?
options: A failed Redis cluster's misses spread across all database shards
Redis supports more shards than MySQL does
It lets each database shard skip invalidation
It keeps hot keys on the same node as their rows
mcq.why: Each Redis cluster holds keys from many database shards, so losing one spreads its misses thinly instead of hammering one shard.

section: 6.10 Uber CacheFront: a cache inside the database
hook: Uber reported 99 percent cache hit rates for its integrated cache. Why read that number carefully?
title: CacheFront: 40M reads/sec, 99.99% measured consistency
body: Uber reported CacheFront's results in 2024: over 40 million reads per second across instances, p75 latency down 75 percent, p99.9 down more than 67 percent, and consistency measured at 99.99 percent. The hit-rate claim needs care: 'up to 99 percent in production cases.' That is a best case, not a fleet average. The broader point is the **integrated cache**: the platform owns invalidation, and every team gets caching for free.
takeaway: 'Up to' is a ceiling, not an average. Read benchmark claims accordingly.
deeper:
**Tail and median together:** p75 down 75 percent and p99.9 down more than 67 percent. When most reads move from storage to memory, the tail improves along with the typical request.

**What 99.99 percent means:** It is what Uber measured with its design in place: direct invalidation, binlog-driven Flux and Lua timestamp checks. It describes that system, not caching in general.

**The cost example:** One CacheFront use case served 6 million reads per second on about 3,000 Redis cores, against an estimated 60,000 database cores.

**Why integrate:** With per-team look-aside, some team eventually forgets a delete, skips the TTL or mishandles a race. When the database platform owns the cache, invalidation comes from the commit log and correctness becomes a platform property. Meta's TAO took a similar route for the social graph.

quiz.q: A vendor slide says 'cache hit rates up to 99 percent,' and your manager plans capacity assuming 99 percent everywhere. What's wrong with that, using CacheFront's own reporting as the example?
quiz.a: 'Up to 99 percent in production cases' is a best case, not an average. Plan with realistic per-workload hit ratios, since each lost percent adds misses to the database.

mcq.q: What is the main advantage of an integrated cache like CacheFront over per-team look-aside caches?
options: The platform owns invalidation, so no app can forget to delete a key
It removes the need for any TTL on cached rows
It guarantees perfect consistency between cache and database
It lets each team choose its own eviction policy
mcq.why: Invalidation comes from the commit log inside the platform, so every team gets correct caching without writing cache logic.

hook: Memcached gives you get, set and delete. What made Redis popular for jobs that aren't caching at all?
title: Redis and Valkey: data structures, not just keys
body: **Redis** is an in-memory data-structure server: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and streams. That makes it useful both as a cache and as a small primary store, for leaderboards, rate limiters and sessions. In 2024 the Linux Foundation community forked it as **Valkey**, which keeps compatibility with the Redis protocol and cluster design. Its cluster design carries over unchanged.
takeaway: Rich data structures make Redis a store. Weak durability limits what it should store.
deeper:
**Beyond get and set:** A sorted set keeps a leaderboard ordered by score. A counter increments atomically for rate limiting. A hash holds a session's fields. Server-side Lua scripts run atomically, which is how Uber's CacheFront implements its timestamp checks against stale fills.

**Where care is needed:** Redis replication is asynchronous and its persistence modes can lose recent writes. Treating it as a durable database just because persistence is on is a classic mistake. Safe primary-store uses are data you can lose or rebuild.

**Proven at scale:** Uber's CacheFront serves over 40 million reads per second backed by Redis.

**Valkey's promise:** Compatibility with the Redis protocol and cluster design means Redis clients and cluster designs carry over to Valkey.

quiz.q: You need a leaderboard ranking a million players by score, updated constantly. Why is Redis a natural fit, and what must be true before making it the only copy?
quiz.a: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score in memory. Before making it the only copy, you must be able to lose or rebuild recent updates, since replication is async and persistence can lose writes.

mcq.q: What is Valkey?
options: A Linux Foundation fork of Redis that keeps its protocol and cluster design
A Redis module that makes replication synchronous
A managed Redis service with a durable write log
A memcached fork with Redis-style data structures
mcq.why: The Linux Foundation community forked Redis as Valkey in 2024, staying compatible with the Redis protocol and cluster design.

hook: Redis multi-key operations need keys on one node. How do you steer related keys onto the same one?
title: 16,384 hash slots, and braces that pin keys together
body: Redis and Valkey cluster mode split the key space into 16,384 **hash slots**. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each primary owns some slots. Multi-key operations need all keys in one slot. **Hash tags** make that possible: if a key contains braces, only the part inside is hashed. So `{user1000}.followers` and `{user1000}.following` land in the same slot and work in one operation.

stat.label: hash slots in a Redis or Valkey cluster

takeaway: Hash the part that matters, and related keys share a home.
deeper:
**Why slots:** They add a fixed layer of indirection. The key-to-slot mapping never changes, since it's just CRC16 mod 16384. Only the slot-to-node mapping changes when nodes join or leave, so rebalancing moves whole slots instead of recomputing every key's home.

**Why tags:** Without them, related keys scatter by their full names and can't be used together. Tags let the application group keys deliberately: everything about user1000 shares a slot.

**The catch:** Everything with the same tag lives in one slot on one node. Tag too much together, or tag a very popular entity, and you've rebuilt the hot-key problem, which sharding can't fix. Use tags only for small groups of keys that genuinely need to be operated on together.

quiz.q: You tag every key in your app with {global} so any multi-key operation works. What problem have you created?
quiz.a: All keys hash to one slot on one node, so a single node takes all the load: a self-made hot spot that no amount of cluster scaling can spread.

mcq.q: How does Redis Cluster compute a key's hash slot?
options: CRC16 of the key, mod 16384
MD5 of the key, mod the node count
CRC32 of the key, mod 1024
Consistent hashing on a Ketama ring
mcq.why: Slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384, or of just the braced part when the key has a hash tag.

hook: A Redis node tells your client 'not here, go there.' When should the client remember it, and when not?
title: MOVED vs ASK: permanent move or one-time detour
body: Redis Cluster clients cache the slot map, so they send each request straight to the owning node. When the map is out of date, the node redirects. A **MOVED** reply means the slot has moved permanently: update the cached map. An **ASK** reply means the slot is migrating: try the other node for just this request, and leave the map alone.
takeaway: MOVED rewrites the map. ASK is a detour for one request.
deeper:
**Why two replies:** Slot migration is gradual. While a slot moves from node A to node B, some of its keys are already on B and some are still on A. A request for a key that has moved gets ASK: go to B for this one. The client must not rewrite its map yet, because other keys in that slot may still be on A.

**When migration ends:** The cluster reassigns the slot, and requests to A get MOVED, telling the client to update permanently.

**Why clients hold the map:** It avoids a proxy hop on every request, much as Meta's clients hash keys to servers and EVCache clients use Ketama.

**Getting it wrong:** A client that treats ASK like MOVED redirects all of a slot's keys to B too early. One that ignores MOVED pays an extra hop on every request.

quiz.q: Mid-migration, your client gets ASK for key k1 in slot 42 and updates its slot map to point slot 42 at the new node. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Other slot-42 keys still live on the old node, so requests for them now go to the wrong node. ASK means redirect only this request and keep the map.

mcq.q: What should a Redis Cluster client do on a MOVED reply?
options: Update its cached slot map to the new node
Retry on the other node for this request only
Wait for migration to finish, then retry
Drop the key from its local cache
mcq.why: MOVED means the slot moved permanently, so the client updates its slot map; ASK is the one-request detour.

hook: Redis told your client the write succeeded. A second later the primary died. Is the write safe?
title: Redis Cluster can lose writes it already acknowledged
body: Each Redis Cluster primary has replicas, but **replication is asynchronous**. The primary acknowledges a write before any replica has it. If the primary then fails and a replica is promoted, that write may never have arrived, so it's gone, even though the client was told it succeeded. The cluster can also lose acknowledged writes on the minority side of a network partition.
takeaway: An acknowledgment from one node is a promise only that node can keep.
deeper:
**Why asynchronous:** Waiting for replicas before acknowledging would add a network round trip to every write, and Redis is built for speed. For a pure cache, losing a few recent writes during failover is harmless, because the data can be read again from the source of truth.

**The partition case:** A network split leaves a primary on the minority side, and clients connected to it keep writing for a while. When the majority side promotes a replica, the minority primary's writes during the split are discarded.

**The guarantee, stated plainly:** Redis Cluster does not guarantee that acknowledged writes survive failover. Add fsync-every-second persistence and it's clear why Redis is not a strongly durable database, whatever its configuration file says about persistence.

quiz.q: Your team stores payment confirmations only in Redis Cluster. A primary crashes at peak. Customers were told their payment was confirmed, but no record exists. Explain how.
quiz.a: The primary acknowledged the confirmation writes, then died before asynchronously replicating them. The promoted replica never saw them, so they vanished despite the acknowledgment.

mcq.q: Why can Redis Cluster lose a write it already acknowledged?
options: Replicas receive writes asynchronously, after the acknowledgment
Writes are buffered in the client until the next fsync
Hash slots are reassigned before writes are applied
The primary acknowledges before writing to its own memory
mcq.why: The primary acknowledges before replicating, so a failover can promote a replica that never got the write.

predict.q: A Redis Cluster primary acknowledges a write, then fails before replicating it. What happens to the write?
options: It can be lost
It is recovered from the replica
It is replayed from the client's buffer

hook: After a crash, Redis might forget one second of writes or several minutes. What decides which?
title: RDB vs AOF: how much Redis forgets after a crash
body: Redis offers several persistence modes. **RDB** snapshots are periodic point-in-time dumps made with `fork()`: compact and fast to restart from, but you can lose minutes of writes, and `fork()` on a big dataset can pause the server briefly. **AOF**, the append-only file, logs every write. With the default fsync every second you lose about one second; fsync always is very safe and very slow. Pure caches often run with no persistence.
takeaway: Your fsync or snapshot interval is your data-loss window.
deeper:
**RDB's trade:** It writes a full snapshot occasionally, so it's cheap during normal operation and loads quickly. Everything since the last snapshot is lost on a crash, and the fork pause matters for latency-sensitive services with large datasets.

**AOF's trade:** Logging each write shrinks the loss window to the fsync interval. Once per second bounds loss to about a second. Syncing on every write makes each one wait for the disk, which gives up most of Redis's speed.

**Both, or neither:** RDB plus AOF gets a compact restart point plus a small loss window. For a pure cache, persistence is often off: the source of truth has the data, and a restart just starts cold.

**The catch:** Persistence on one node does nothing for writes lost to asynchronous replication during failover.

quiz.q: A rate limiter in Redis uses RDB snapshots every 10 minutes, and the node crashes. What's lost, and would AOF with fsync every second change the picture?
quiz.a: Up to about 10 minutes of counter updates since the last snapshot. AOF with fsync every second shrinks that to about one second, at the cost of logging every write.

mcq.q: With AOF and the default fsync every second, roughly how much data can Redis lose on a crash?
options: About one second of writes
Several minutes of writes
Nothing, every write is on disk
Everything since the last RDB snapshot
mcq.why: The default fsyncs the log once per second, so up to about a second of logged writes may not be on disk yet.

hook: Persistence is on and the AOF is writing. So your Redis is a durable database now. Right?
title: Persistence on doesn't make Redis a durable database
body: Persistence and replication answer different questions. Persistence: if this node restarts, how much of its data comes back? Replication: if this node dies, does another node have everything it acknowledged? Redis persistence answers the first partially and the second not at all. **Asynchronous replication** plus fsync every second means a failover can lose recent writes. Use Redis as a primary store only for data you can lose or rebuild.
takeaway: Durability is two questions: restart and failover. Persistence answers only one.
deeper:
**How the write disappears:** A primary acknowledges a write and fails before replicating it. Its own AOF may even hold the write, but the replica that gets promoted never saw it, so the cluster moves on without it.

**Where Redis is fine:** Rate-limiter counts, leaderboards you can recompute, sessions users can recreate. Losing a second or two of writes, or rebuilding the data, is acceptable.

**Where it's dangerous:** Data of record: account balances, orders, anything a user expects to survive once confirmed.

**If you must:** Use a managed variant with a durable log, and read the fine print; its guarantees only help if you verify them. The rule underneath: Redis/Valkey Cluster uses asynchronous replication, and persistence doesn't make it strongly durable.

quiz.q: A teammate enables AOF with fsync always on a Redis Cluster primary and declares orders safe. What failure can still lose an acknowledged order?
quiz.a: A failover. Replication is asynchronous, so if the primary dies before its replica receives the order, the promoted replica lacks it, whatever the old primary's disk holds.

mcq.q: Which data is a safe fit for Redis as the only primary store?
options: Rate-limiter counts that can be lost or rebuilt
Customer account balances after each payment
Order confirmations shown to customers
Legal records that must never be lost
mcq.why: Async replication and periodic fsync can lose recent writes, so only data you can lose or rebuild belongs in Redis alone.

hook: For images and video, the biggest cache in the system isn't near the database at all. Where is it?
title: The CDN: the biggest cache sits next to the user
body: For large blobs like images, video and JavaScript, the biggest cache is near the user, not the database. A **content delivery network** (CDN) is a set of cache servers in many cities and inside internet providers. Akamai and Cloudflare sell this as a service; Meta runs its own edge caches. The CacheLib paper (2020) reports that Meta's CDN caches serve 70 percent of web requests and cut latency by an order of magnitude.

stat.label: of Meta's web requests served by its CDN caches

takeaway: The origin keeps everything. The edge keeps what's popular, close to users.
deeper:
**What a CDN saves:** Database caches save CPU and database load. A CDN mainly saves distance and bandwidth. A user fetching an image from a server in their own city, or inside their own provider's network, gets it far faster than from a distant data center, and the long-haul network carries far less.

**Same shape, different layer:** The origin, an object store, holds everything durably. The CDN serves the popular part near users. It's the same source-of-truth-plus-disposable-copy relationship as a database and memcache.

**Tied to CacheLib:** The CDN was one of the separate caching systems whose common core CacheLib unified. Its traffic was also one of the workloads measured as flatter than textbook Zipf, around alpha 0.55, with popularity shifting over hours, a push toward larger caches that include flash.

quiz.q: Why is an object store plus a CDN the same pattern as a database plus memcache, just at a different layer?
quiz.a: In both, a durable origin holds all data as the source of truth, and a disposable copy of the popular part serves reads faster; losing the copy costs speed, not data.

mcq.q: What does a CDN mainly save compared with caches near the database?
options: Distance and network bandwidth to users
Database CPU spent parsing SQL
Flash wear on origin storage servers
Invalidation traffic from the commit log
mcq.why: CDN servers sit in many cities and inside ISPs, so popular blobs travel a short path instead of crossing the long-haul network.

hook: Most caches wait for a request. Netflix fills its caches before anyone asks. How can it?
title: Open Connect: Netflix fills the cache before anyone asks
body: Netflix built its own CDN, **Open Connect**. It places Open Connect Appliances in its own 60+ data centers and, for free, inside more than a thousand partner ISPs. Netflix knows in advance what people are likely to watch, so it fills the appliances during off-peak hours, called nightly fills. This is **proactive caching**: the cache is filled before any request, which only works when the catalog is known and changes slowly.
takeaway: If you can predict demand, fill the cache before demand arrives.
deeper:
**Inverting demand-fill:** Most caches are demand-filled: data enters when someone misses on it. Open Connect decides ahead of time which titles each location needs. Loading them overnight uses network capacity when it's otherwise idle, so peak-hour viewing is served from nearby appliances.

**Why free placement works:** An appliance inside an ISP puts content as close to viewers as possible, and the ISP no longer has to carry that traffic in from far away.

**Where it breaks:** Only with a known, slowly changing catalog. A social feed, with new posts every second and popularity shifting within hours, cannot be pre-filled this way.

**A Netflix habit:** EVCache's cross-region replication follows the same instinct. Fill caches before traffic needs them, so they're warm at the critical moment.

quiz.q: A news site wants to copy Netflix's nightly-fill approach for its breaking-news pages. Why won't that work well?
quiz.a: Proactive filling needs a known, slowly changing catalog. Breaking news appears unpredictably and popularity shifts within hours, so the site can't know tonight what to pre-fill for tomorrow.

mcq.q: What makes Netflix's proactive nightly fills possible?
options: A known catalog that changes slowly, with predictable viewing
ISPs paying Netflix to host the appliances
Appliances that fetch each title on its first request
Kafka replicating every title across regions nightly
mcq.why: Netflix knows what's likely to be watched, so it can load appliances off-peak before requests arrive.

hook: Your hit ratio slips from 99 to 95 percent. Sounds like a rounding error. What does the database see?
title: 99% to 95% hit ratio means 5× the database load
body: Database load equals read rate × (1 − hit ratio), so the **miss rate** is what matters. Take an illustrative peak of 2 million reads per second and a database safe at 100,000. At 99 percent, 20,000 reads reach the database. At 98, 40,000. At 95, 100,000: five times the load, right at the limit. At 90, 200,000: overload. A cache at 99 percent is load-bearing, because a partial failure to 95 is a database outage.
takeaway: Hit ratio flatters you. Miss rate is what the database pays.
deeper:
**Flip the number:** 99 and 95 sound close. As misses, 1 percent versus 5 percent is a factor of five. Always reason about the miss rate.

**Smaller drops still bite:** A hit ratio falling from 99 to 97 percent after a deploy means misses go from 1 percent to 3 percent of reads. Database read load triples.

**The same math values improvements:** Every 1 percent of hit ratio gained removes 20,000 database reads per second at peak in this example. That's what justifies spending on bigger caches, flash tiers and warmup machinery.

**The cascade:** Cache nodes restart or fail, hit ratio drops from say 99 to 90, database load rises 10 times, latency and timeouts climb, clients retry, and more load follows. Every mitigation in caching attacks one link in that chain.

quiz.q: After a deploy, your hit ratio drops from 99.5 to 98.5 percent. The team calls it noise. How much did database read load change?
quiz.a: It tripled: misses went from 0.5 percent to 1.5 percent of reads. Database load follows the miss rate, not the hit rate.

mcq.q: At 2 million reads/sec, what hit ratio puts 100,000 reads/sec on the database?
options: 95 percent
99 percent
90 percent
98 percent
mcq.why: Misses = 2,000,000 × (1 − 0.95) = 100,000 reads per second.

predict.q: Hit ratio drops from 99% to 95% at 2 million reads/sec. How does database load change?
options: It rises 5×
It rises about 4%
It doubles

hook: Memory math says about 11 cache servers. Throughput math says something else. Which number do you buy?
title: Size a cache for memory and throughput; buy the larger
body: Illustrative numbers: 200 million daily users, each profile about 1 KB plus 100 bytes of overhead. Memory: about 220 GB per copy, 660 GB for one copy in each of three zones, roughly 11 servers in total at 64 GB each. Throughput: at 200,000 gets per second per server, 2 million reads per second per zone copy needs at least 10 servers per zone, perhaps 15 with failure headroom. **Throughput** wins by roughly 3-4×.
takeaway: Hold the hot set and serve the peak. Buy for whichever is harder.
deeper:
**Memory, step by step:**
1. 200 million × 1.1 KB is about 220 GB per copy.
2. One copy per zone in three zones: about 660 GB.
3. At 64 GB usable per server: about 11 servers in total, under 4 per zone.

**Throughput:** The example sizes each zone's copy for the full 2 million reads per second peak. 2 million per second at 200,000 per server is 10 servers per zone minimum. Headroom for failures brings it to perhaps 15 per zone.

**Reading the comparison:** The two can look similar (11 versus 10), but that compares a three-zone memory total with a per-zone throughput minimum. Per zone, throughput needs roughly three to four times more servers, so it decides. When they differ, size for the larger.

**Why both checks:** Memory-only estimates undersize high-QPS caches of small items. Throughput-only estimates undersize caches of large items.

quiz.q: A cache holds 50 TB of large video thumbnails but serves only 100,000 reads/sec. Which sizing check likely decides the server count, and why?
quiz.a: Memory. Large items fill RAM long before a modest read rate saturates servers, so the memory estimate gives the larger count.

mcq.q: When memory-based and throughput-based sizing give different server counts, which should you use?
options: The larger count
The smaller count
Their average
The memory count, since RAM costs most
mcq.why: The cache must both hold the hot set and serve peak requests with failure headroom; falling short on either hurts hit ratio or latency.

predict.q: An illustrative cache needs about 660 GB across 3 zones and 2 million reads/sec per zone. Which sets the server count?
options: Throughput
Memory
They match exactly

hook: Daily active users already fit in DRAM. Why would you pay for flash to cache everyone else too?
title: Every 1% of hit ratio is 20,000 database reads/sec
body: In the illustrative example, DRAM holds the 200 million daily actives. The other 800 million users' profiles miss and go to the database: individually rare, collectively large. The full set is 1 billion × 1.1 KB, about 1.1 TB. If that fits in a few **flash-backed** servers, the long tail hits flash instead of the database. At a 2 million read peak, every 1 percent of hit ratio gained removes 20,000 database reads per second.

stat.label: DB reads/sec saved per 1% of hit ratio

takeaway: The long tail is rare per user and huge in total. Cache it cheaply.
deeper:
**Where the misses come from:** A DRAM cache sized for daily actives serves them well. Everyone else misses. The CacheLib paper found real popularity flatter than textbook Zipf, which makes such tails large.

**Why flash fits:** It offers many times more capacity per dollar than DRAM with sub-millisecond reads. If all 1.1 TB fits on a few flash-backed servers, tail misses become flash hits.

**Scale the gain:** Database load equals read rate × (1 − hit ratio). Each percent is 20,000 reads per second, against a database whose safe limit in the example is 100,000. A few points of hit ratio is a large share of that budget.

**The costs to weigh:** Flash endurance, managed with admission policies, and slightly slower flash hits than DRAM.

quiz.q: Your DRAM cache runs at 96 percent hit ratio at 2 million reads/sec. A flash tier would lift it to 98. How many database reads per second does that remove, and is it significant against a 100,000/sec limit?
quiz.a: 40,000 per second (2 points × 20,000). That's 40 percent of the database's safe capacity, so yes, very significant.

mcq.q: In the example, why can flash reduce database load even though daily actives fit in DRAM?
options: Rarely active users miss DRAM, and flash can hold their profiles cheaply
Flash reads are faster than DRAM for small profiles
Flash removes the need to replicate profiles per zone
Daily actives are evicted from DRAM during failover
mcq.why: The 800 million less-active users miss a DRAM cache sized for daily actives; caching the full 1.1 TB on flash turns those misses into hits.

hook: A fleet-wide deploy restarts every cache node. Nothing crashes. The database still goes down. Why?
title: Restart many cache nodes at once and the database floods
body: A restarted memcached node comes back empty. Restart many at once, as in a fleet-wide deploy, and the database sees a surge of misses it may not survive. That's the **cold cache** failure mode. The fixes: roll restarts slowly so only a small fraction is cold at a time, restart warm (CacheLib), warm new clusters from a warm peer (Meta), and replicate across regions (EVCache, CacheFront).
takeaway: A deploy is a cache outage unless you design it not to be.
deeper:
**The math of cold:** If a cache normally runs at 99 percent and a deploy empties a tenth of it, the effective hit ratio can fall toward 90 percent. In the illustrative example that's ten times the database load, far past its limit.

**Each fix targets a different cause:** Slow rolling restarts limit how much is cold at any moment, trading deploy speed for safety. Warm restarts avoid emptying the cache at all. Cold Cluster Warmup fills brand-new clusters from a warm peer in hours instead of days. Cross-region replication covers the biggest case: a whole region's traffic moving elsewhere.

**Routine, not rare:** Many production caches run less than 7 days between restarts. Restarts are a routine operation, so they must be designed never to look like an outage to the database.

quiz.q: Your deploy tool restarts cache nodes in batches of 50 percent to finish fast. Afterward the database struggles for an hour. Suggest two fixes that don't slow feature delivery much.
quiz.a: Warm restarts, so nodes reattach saved state and come back full, and warming from a peer. Or shrink batches to roll restarts slowly so little of the cache is cold at once.

mcq.q: Why does restarting many memcached nodes at once endanger the database?
options: Restarted nodes come back empty, so misses surge
Restarted nodes lose their invalidation logs
Clients rehash every key onto the Gutter pool
Restarted nodes serve stale data until warmed
mcq.why: An empty node misses on everything it owned, so a mass restart drops hit ratio sharply and floods the database.

hook: DynamoDB's routers call the backend even when their cache hits. On purpose. Why waste the work?
title: DynamoDB keeps its backend busy even on cache hits
body: Normally a high hit ratio lets the backend fleet shrink. Then caches suddenly go ineffective and the backend faces load it was never sized for. The DynamoDB paper warns against letting caches hide that work. Its request routers cache partition metadata locally, but even on a hit they send an asynchronous refresh to the **MemDS** metadata fleet. MemDS serves a constant volume regardless of hit ratio. That costs extra load normally and prevents cascading failures.
takeaway: If the backend never relies on the cache, losing the cache is a non-event.
deeper:
**The trap it avoids:** A cache as a hidden capacity dependency. Hit ratio rises, the backend is sized for misses, and a mass restart or access-pattern change sends a spike it can't take.

**Constant work:** Because the routers' refresh calls go out whether or not they hit, MemDS load never depends on hit ratio. There's no spike to survive, because MemDS already handles the full volume every day.

**The price:** It deliberately gives up offload on this path. Extra load in normal times buys stability in bad times.

**If you can't do that:** Keep the database able to survive a realistic miss storm, or add admission control and load shedding in front of it so overload is refused gracefully instead of cascading. DynamoDB answered 'could the backend survive an empty cache?' with a permanent yes.

quiz.q: Your metadata service runs nearly idle behind a 98 percent hit-ratio cache, and finance wants to shrink it. How would DynamoDB's design change that conversation?
quiz.a: DynamoDB routers refresh from MemDS even on hits, so MemDS always carries full load and is sized for it. There's no hidden headroom to cut, and cache loss causes no spike.

mcq.q: Why do DynamoDB's request routers call MemDS even on a cache hit?
options: So MemDS load stays constant and never spikes when caches fail
So the cached metadata is always fully consistent with MemDS
