So MemDS can measure which partitions are hot
So the routers can skip their local cache entirely
mcq.why: Constant refresh traffic keeps MemDS sized for full load, so ineffective caches cause no sudden spike or cascade.

hook: One cache node dies. Minutes later three more are down, one after another. What's knocking them over?
title: Failure rehashing: one dead node, then the next
body: When a node dies in a consistent-hashing cluster, its keys typically rehash onto survivors. That assumes keys are equal units of load. They're not: Meta observed a single key taking 20 percent of a server's requests. If the dead node held a hot key, its new owner takes a sudden surge, may overload and die, and passes the keys onward. That's **failure rehashing**, a cascade. Meta's Gutter pool avoids it.
takeaway: Rehashing assumes keys weigh the same. Hot keys prove they don't.
deeper:
**The chain, step by step:**
1. Node A dies.
2. Its hot key rehashes to node B.
3. B overloads and dies.
4. Its keys, including the hot one, move to node C.

**How Gutter breaks the chain:** About 1 percent of servers stay idle. When a server fails, clients send its traffic to Gutter instead of rehashing it onto neighbors, so no healthy server's load changes. Gutter entries expire quickly. The result was a 99 percent cut in client-visible failures.

**Replication helps too:** With replicated pools or per-zone copies as in EVCache, losing one copy of a hot key leaves others still serving it.

**The design lesson:** Spare capacity reserved for failures beats spreading failures over already busy servers.

quiz.q: Your cache cluster runs every node near capacity. One node holding a viral post's key dies, and consistent hashing moves the key to a neighbor. Predict what happens and name one fix.
quiz.a: The neighbor absorbs the hot key on top of its own load, overloads, dies, and pushes load onward in a cascade. Fix: route a failed node's traffic to an idle Gutter pool.

mcq.q: What makes failure rehashing risky?
options: Load per key is uneven, so a hot key can overload its new owner
Rehashing invalidates every key in the cluster at once
Consistent hashing moves all keys, not just the dead node's
Rehashed keys lose their TTLs and never expire
mcq.why: A moved hot key can push a healthy node over capacity, which fails and passes the load on, cascading.

hook: The original fault is fixed, yet the database stays pinned. Something your clients do keeps it there. What?
title: Retry storms: timeouts that multiply the load
body: Clients that retry cache timeouts against the database, or retry database timeouts repeatedly, add load exactly when the system is struggling. Load grows as things get worse, and the loop can keep a database overloaded after the trigger is gone. The fix: cap **retries**, use backoff, and treat cache errors as misses only when the database can take it. Meta's clients skip the cache fill after a UDP get error to avoid adding load.
takeaway: A retry is extra load you send at the worst possible moment.
deeper:
**Last link of the cascade:**
1. Cache nodes restart or fail.
2. Hit ratio drops.
3. Database load rises.
4. Latency and timeouts climb.
5. Clients retry, and load rises further.

**What each fix does:** Capping retries bounds how much one request can amplify load. Backoff spreads retries in time so they don't arrive as a synchronized wave.

**The quiet default:** Treating cache errors as misses is standard look-aside behavior, but it silently converts every cache problem into database load. It's only safe when the database has headroom.

**Load-aware by design:** Meta's clients still get the value after a UDP get error, but don't add a set to a cache that may be congested. Leases, request coalescing and load shedding help at the same stage by removing duplicate queries and refusing excess work gracefully.

quiz.q: During an incident, your clients retry every failed database call immediately, up to 5 times. The database recovers briefly, then collapses again. Why, and what two changes help most?
quiz.a: Each failure spawns up to 5 immediate retries, multiplying load right when the database is weakest. Cap retries and add backoff so retries are fewer and spread out.

mcq.q: What does a Meta client do after a UDP get error, to avoid adding load?
options: Skips the cache fill after reading the database
Retries the get immediately over TCP
Marks the cache server as dead
Serves a stale value from the Gutter pool
mcq.why: The client gets the value but doesn't write it back, since the error may mean congestion and a set would add load.

hook: A cache entry has been wrong for three months, and nothing will ever fix it. How does that happen?
title: A missed invalidation with no TTL lives forever
body: A delete lost to an app crash, dropped by the network, or undone by a stale set leaves a wrong value in the cache. If nothing forces it out, it stays indefinitely. Users see old data with no end in sight, and the bug is hard to trace because the code that caused it ran long ago. The fix is almost embarrassingly simple: always set a **TTL**.
takeaway: A TTL turns a permanent data bug into a temporary one.
deeper:
**Why teams skip TTLs:** They already invalidate on write, so a TTL seems redundant. Or they want the highest possible hit ratio.

**Why that fails:** Invalidation can break at least three ways: stale sets, replication-lag refills and lost deletes. Even commit-log invalidators like McSqueal and Flux can miss a key through a bug in key extraction or a write path that bypasses them.

**What a TTL does:** It prevents none of those, but it caps the damage. A stale entry is wrong for at most the TTL, not forever.

**The cost, and its fixes:** Some extra misses as entries expire. Spread them with jitter so keys don't expire together, and protect hot keys with leases, coalescing or early refresh. That's a small price compared with data that never corrects itself.

quiz.q: An audit finds a handful of profiles showing names changed months ago. Your system uses McSqueal-style invalidation and no TTLs. Give a plausible cause and the one change that caps it.
quiz.a: An invalidation was missed, for example through a key-extraction bug or a stale set. With no TTL the entries never expire. Add a TTL so any such error lasts at most one TTL.

mcq.q: Why is a missing TTL dangerous even if you invalidate on every write?
options: Any failed invalidation leaves a stale entry that never expires
Entries without a TTL are evicted first under memory pressure
Invalidations are ignored for keys that have no TTL
Keys without a TTL cannot be replicated across zones
mcq.why: Invalidations can fail through lost deletes, stale sets or replica refills; without expiry, those wrong values stay forever.

hook: Each cache read is fast almost every time. A page that makes 500 of them is slow almost every time. Why?
title: A 500-key page waits for its slowest key
body: A page that fetches 500 keys can't render until the slowest of those 500 responses arrives. If each read has only a small chance of being slow, a request touching hundreds of keys very likely includes one. So page latency follows the tail, not the average. That's the cost of **fan-out**. Large values make it worse, and many responses arriving at once cause incast congestion. The fix: batch requests, cap fan-out, and watch incast.
takeaway: Fan-out turns rare slowness into common slowness.
deeper:
**Meta lives here:** A Meta page load can fetch hundreds of keys, so its latency depends on fan-out.

**Large values add pressure:** Each large response takes longer to transfer and fills network buffers faster. Many arriving together at one web server can overflow switch buffers, the incast congestion Meta handles with a sliding window of outstanding requests.

**Structural fixes:**
1. Batch many keys per request to the same server, cutting round trips.
2. Cap fan-out with pages and data models that need fewer keys, or group related data so it fetches together, such as Redis hash tags that place related keys in one slot.
3. Monitor for incast, which shows up as packet loss and latency spikes rather than clean errors.

quiz.q: Each cache read is slow 1 time in 1,000. A page does 500 reads in parallel. Roughly how often does the page wait on at least one slow read, and what do you change?
quiz.a: About 40 percent of the time (1 − 0.999^500 ≈ 0.39). Cut fan-out: batch keys per server, group related data, and fetch fewer keys per page.

mcq.q: Why does a page fetching 500 cache keys suffer more than average per-key latency suggests?
options: It waits for the slowest of 500 responses
Each key adds its full latency in sequence
The cache throttles clients that fetch many keys
Large pages bypass the cache and read the database
mcq.why: Parallel reads finish when the last one does, so the page's latency tracks the tail of 500 draws, not the average.

hook: Nobody touched your service's code. Its database load jumped anyway, the day another team shipped. How?
title: Eviction surprises: a new feature evicts your valuable keys
body: A new feature starts writing many low-value keys into a shared cache. Memory fills, the eviction policy pushes out older entries, and some were valuable, frequently read keys serving another workload. That workload's hit ratio falls and its database load rises, though its code never changed. The fix is **isolation**: separate pools, as at Meta, or separate clusters per workload, so one workload's churn can't destroy another's cache.
takeaway: In a shared cache, your hit ratio belongs to whoever writes the most.
deeper:
**Damage far from the cause:** The team shipping the feature sees nothing wrong. The team whose database runs hot sees no change in their own code. Because small hit-ratio drops multiply database load, evicting even a few percent of another workload's hot set can hurt. In an illustrative example, 99 to 95 percent is five times the database load.

**How Meta isolates:** Pools give each workload its own servers and memory, and mcrouter routes keys to the right pool by key prefix. A low-value, high-churn key set can't evict valuable keys elsewhere. Separate clusters per workload do the same at a coarser grain.

**Sizing gets easier too:** Each pool can be sized by its own memory and throughput needs.

**A cousin inside one cache:** Twitter's slab calcification, memory stuck in stale size classes, was fixed with Twemcache's slab-level eviction.

quiz.q: Your hit ratio fell from 99 to 96 percent overnight and database load quadrupled. Your code didn't change, but another team launched a feature on the same cache cluster. What likely happened, and what prevents a repeat?
quiz.a: Their feature wrote many low-value keys that evicted your hot keys. Isolate workloads with separate pools, routed by key prefix, or separate clusters.

mcq.q: What is the recommended fix for eviction surprises?
options: Separate pools or clusters per workload
Longer TTLs on every valuable key
A larger shared cache for all workloads
Write-through caching for the new feature
mcq.why: Isolation keeps one workload's low-value churn from evicting another workload's hot keys.

hook: A few cache nodes restart. An hour later the database is melting. What happened in between?
title: The cache failure cascade, and where to cut it
body: Cache failures cascade in a predictable chain. Nodes restart or fail. Hit ratio drops, say from 99 to 90 percent. Database load rises tenfold. Latency and timeouts climb. Clients retry, adding more load. Each link can be cut. **Gutter pools**, warm restarts and cold cluster warmup keep hit ratio up. Leases, request coalescing and load shedding protect the database. Capped retries with backoff stop the loop.
takeaway: Every caching technique cuts the same chain. Know which link it cuts.
deeper:
**Stage one, capacity lost:** Meta's Gutter pool absorbs failed servers' traffic. CacheLib warm restarts keep deployed nodes full. Cold Cluster Warmup fills new clusters from warm peers. Slow rolling restarts limit how much is cold at once. Cross-region replication (EVCache, CacheFront) keeps failover regions warm.

**Stage two, database surge:** Leases let one client per key refill, cutting Meta's herd-prone peak from 17,000 to 1,300 queries per second. Request coalescing merges duplicate misses. Load shedding and admission control refuse excess work gracefully. Serving stale on error avoids the database entirely.

**Stage three, retries:** Cap them, add backoff, and treat cache errors as misses only when the database can take it.

**At design time:** Ask whether the database could survive if this cache were empty. DynamoDB's constant refresh to MemDS is the extreme answer: make backend load independent of hit ratio.

quiz.q: You can fund one project: warm restarts for the cache fleet, or request coalescing in the app tier. Which cascade stage does each protect, and which prevents the surge in the first place?
quiz.a: Warm restarts act before the surge, keeping hit ratio up through deploys. Coalescing acts after, trimming duplicate database queries. Warm restarts prevent the surge; coalescing only softens it.

mcq.q: Which mitigation acts before database load rises in the cache failure cascade?
options: Gutter pool
Load shedding
Request coalescing
Retry backoff
mcq.why: The Gutter pool keeps hit ratio up when nodes fail; the others protect the database after load has already risen.
